records.text: ario where we assumed that after 15 years (with the Generational Fund rolling over three times) the balance distribution in AFPs remains unchanged across different age groups. In this scenario, where the only changing variable is the shift in age distribution (Figure 6), the Generational Fund regime would naturally adopt a more conservative asset allocation (Figure 7). As a result, AFPs might need to divest foreign assets and increase their holdings of local government bonds to comply with the investment limits. In terms of FX implications, the introduction of the new regime is unlikely to trigger any significant impact, as AFPs' current foreign holdings are already within the new limits. As a result, there is no clear direct impact on the USDCLP or the CLP basis. However, if the ageing of main contributors leads to a decline in demand for foreign holdings, as investment appetites become more conservative, this could result in reduced USD buying and FX selling by AFPs, which in turn could support the CLP and lead to a higher CLP basis. In the near term, the low carry on the peso could expose it to USD strengthening more noticeably than its peers, with the upside risk of the USD and the likely continuation of the CLP's funding status pointing towards CLP underperforming its peers. The BoJ left its policy rate on hold for almost a year – between its January and December 2025 hikes – due to concerns over potential fallout from the Trump administration's reciprocal tariffs. As the negative impact proved to be minimal, with the benefit of hindsight, it is difficult to see why normalisation did not resume in summer 2025. A ‘catch-up’ phase would have been warranted then, but the onset of the Middle East crisis in late February pushed the BoJ to hold off until June, even after the March confirmation that wage growth was set to exceed 5% for the third year in a row. Risk of two further rate hikes before the end of 2026: What should be the pace of rate hikes now? If the BoJ hikes in September and December this year, the policy rate would rise to 1.5%, roughly on par with the 1.38– 1.63% range consistent with underlying inflation of 1.75% (approaching 2%) as indicated by our simplified Taylor rule. Once the policy rate reaches 1.5%, a single additional hike would align it roughly with the neutral nominal rate (1.75–2.0%) consistent with the 2% inflation target, thereby providing the BoJ with greater policy space. Our base case differs. We believe that the BoJ is most likely to hike just once in 2026, in October. We consider this realistic, given that the central bank has trodden cautiously thus far and faces significant political constraints. The Indian Rupee Non-Deliverable Forward (NDF) and Swap (NDS) market is one of the largest NDF markets in the world. It exists because the Indian rupee (INR) remains only partially convertible; onshore forward access requires documented underlying exposure and approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Therefore, offshore corporates, global banks, foreign hedge funds, macro traders, and others use the NDF market to hedge or speculate on INR movements. What drives the NDS market? Indian corporates and banks that raise money abroad typically pay Mumbai Interbank Forward Offer Rate (MIFOR) swaps to hedge their forward USDINR risk and meet their USD needs when the bonds or loans mature. Additionally, Yaskawa Electric's earnings decline from March to May, caused by system migration issues, weighed on sentiment. Furthermore, an accelerated R&D and mass-production spending on AI robotics in the US and China has increased competitive pressure on Japanese robotics firms. METI views Japan’s core strengths as the supply chain for components (motors, reducers, sensors), materials and equipment as well as operational expertise in control, safety design, maintenance and quality management, cultivated through years of on-site implementation. Arguably this has aided the central bank in its push to drive expectations lower. We observe some early evidence that this dynamic is gradually changing, however. Expectations still sensitive: The sensitivity of inflation expectations to past inflation is at a much lower level than pre-Covid – again consistent with our finding that South Africa does not have an inflation persistency problem (see page 2). Software stocks have underperformed year-to-date, partly due to concerns that AI could replace vendor solutions, reflected in reports of Starbucks moving from Microsoft and IBM platforms to in-house software. We see limited risks to Japanese system integrators (SIs) such as Fujitsu, NEC and NRI, because of a domestic shortage of IT talent and the mission-critical, highly customized nature of the companies’ core systems. BayCurrent’s 15 July results indicated increased demand for consulting in cybersecurity and defense. Domestic SIs with manufacturing expertise are expected to pivotal to implementing physical AI, as in Fujitsu’s 16 July partnerships with three leading robotics companies. Is the automotive sector less precarious than feared? The automotive sector in Japan has faced pressure on its profits since the start of the year, driven by higher raw-material costs and potential impact on demand from tensions in the Middle-East. Nonetheless, April-to-June results could show resilience, with reports of double-digit growth of new Japanese-brand car sales in the US in June. The USDJPY rate remaining above 160 provides a currency tailwind. Several automotive stocks offer dividend yields above 4%, indicating defensive characteristics in a risk-off environment. records.text: LS VIEW ▼ Gold found a consistent level of support at around USD4,000/oz over the last month, after struggling in response to a switch to US rate-hike expectations and, in particular, to the hawkish tone adopted by new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh in his first Fed meeting last month. Support has continued to come from the official sector, with robust central bank buying over the last couple of months, a trend we expect to continue. Strong physical investor demand in Asia, and China in particular, has also helped sustain prices above USD4,000/oz. Over the next month, we expect gold to trade largely sideways as rate- hike expectations cap the upside. However, we remain bullish for the longer term as elevated sovereign debt, sustained US policy uncertainty, and de-dollarisation trends remain in place. 3517/07/2026 Aldo Spanjer PhD, Head of Commodity Strategy | Jason Ying, Commodities Desk Strategist | Elena Lee, Commodities Desk Strategist | BNP Paribas London Branch | David Wilson, Head of Metals Strategy | BNP Paribas Singapore Branch Commodities: Energy back in the spotlight Formatting checked

In addition to having plenty of risk narratives from other markets to pivot around , currency traders are also focused on how to think about the JPY and the potential for intervention to strengthen it. But in terms of known unknowns, it’s harder to find one more adequately priced – short-dated USDJPY risk reverals carry one of the strongest skews for puts of the last five years. The value looks to be in playing for USDJPY downside in longer da ted options, where skew is actually near its least expensive levels in five years. USDJPY liquidity has been amongst the strongest of any pair over the last week and month, with only USDZAR rivalling it for relative health. records.text: t that China’s economic growth remains highly bifurcated (see China economic tracker: Growth remains bifurcated, dated 1 July). Exports remained the main engine, with container throughput at major ports up 5.2% y/y in the first 22 days of June. By contrast, domestic consumption stayed lukewarm due to an unfavourable base effect and the scaling back of subsidies. The property sector also showed signs of cooling: new-home sales in 31 select cities fell 4.1% in June, versus a 1.8% decline in May, while growth in second-hand housing transactions in nine select cities slipped to 6.6% y/y in June from 19.7% in May. Taken together with the April–May official economic data, we anticipate a significant slowdown in China’s GDP growth to roughly 4.4% y/y in Q2 from 5.0% in Q1. However, we still believe the PBoC is unlikely to deliver an immediate cut to the policy rate or the RRR, as the Q2 slowdown primarily reflects an unfavourable base effect and a slower fiscal spending pace. We expect these headwinds to ease in Q3 as fiscal expenditure and government bond issuance accelerate, while the statistical bases for retail sales and FAI become more supportive. Further, given the tepid credit demand, banks’ persistently low net interest margins will continue to constrain the PBoC from reducing rates, in our view. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 3 July 2026 1 Insights Classification: Premium Material D M Inf lation In Focu s : Beep, beep, beep INFLATION TRENDS. A month ago, the beeping was inflation alarm bells going off; today, it is the sound of reversing vehicles — or at least their fuel prices. Retail fuel prices do not move quite as violently as oil markets, but they do follow them closely. Just as pass -through was quick and uneven on the way up, so it will be on the way down. In Australia, thanks to policy interventions, vehicle fuel prices are already below their end -February starting point. In the US, they may be 20% off their peak, but still have much further to fall (Figure 1). This almost guarantees the peak in developed -market inflation is behind us, but it does not mean inflation rates will fall evenly, leaving inflation as a likely source of policy dispersion. US. According to State Street PriceStats, the annual inflation rate peaked on 31 st May at just over 5%. It has fallen sharply since. Over June, the US price level declined by 18bps, pointing firmly to a very soft official reading (Figure 1). This mark s the sharpest monthly decline in 31 months and the largest recorded June fall since our data began in 2008. With June typically delivering a seasonal price rise of between 0.2% and 0.3%, this implies an even larger 50bps fall in the annual inflation rate. Online prices and official inflation fell sharply during 2022 -24, driven primarily by favo urable terms-of-trade dynamics and base effects. The fuel and food price shocks that pushed inflation above target reversed, transport inflation turned negative, food inflation moderated, and supply chain pressures eased. Crucially, the SARB’s restrictive p olicy stance prevented these shocks from feeding into a sustained wage and core inflation cycle. Importantly, the SARB eased only cautiously. A roughly 500bp decline in inflation was met by just 100bp of rate cuts, preserving elevated real interest rates and supporting the rand. A similar dynamic is evident today. Far from a freefall: While current market narratives paint a picture of a labour market in freefall, we believe such pessimism may be a misinterpretation of a post-policy recalibration. The immediate post-pandemic period was marked by tightness in the labour market, but since 2022 there has been a material cooling. However, we see this not as a labour market on the brink of collapse, but rather one that has recalibrated in response to monetary and fiscal policy changes and normalised to historical levels. At USD12.5bn, the 2x SK Hynix ETF has become one of the largest ETFs on the Hong Kong stock exchange, while the AUM of the 2x Samsung Electronics ETF has reached USD3.4bn. On 27 May, a series of 2x single-stock ETFs were introduced on the Korea Exchange, tracking the same two firms. The aggregate daily AUM of the 2x Samsung Electronics product and the 2x SK Hynix ETF have been at USD3.4bn and USD5.5bn respectively in the month since launch. Across both exchanges, the total AUM of Samsung and SK Hynix 2x single-stock ETFs represents 0.6% and 1.5% respectively of the firms’ market capitalizations. Investors have been trading 2x ETFs tracking broad-based indices (e.g. local benchmarks) and specific sectors (e.g. semiconductors) in the North Asian markets for some time, but we think it may take a while for market participants to fully embrace the pricing dynamics and volatility profile of 2x single-stock ETFs, given the positions tend to be more concentrated versus index/sector products. Given its popularity with retail investors in the US, investors will likely continue to favour levered ETFs in APAC as well. However, some regional regulators could increase their oversight and/or be more selective in launching new products as suggested by the recent comments from Korea’s Financial Supervisory Service.

records.text: mberg Historically, whenever the 12m moving average for payrolls is at current levels (42k) , the US has been in recession and the unemployment rate has been climbing. Now, we are talking about growth upgrades and , at 4.2% the unemployment rate has only been lower than current levels just prior to the Dot Com crash and, the pandemic. This time really is different. A shrinking US workforce effectively means that the replacement rate for payrolls (i.e. the number of monthly job gains needed to maintain the labour market balance) is now negative. This is somewhat difficult to conceptualise, so lets just call the replac ement rate zero. What this means is that any monthly rise in payrolls actually tightens the labour market and hence, should be seen, at the margin, as hawkish for the Fed. However, excluding policy factors, inflation has now exceeded 2% for more than four years, and spring labor negotiations have resulted in wage growth of over 3% for three consecutive years. Against this backdrop, corporate pricing behavior has fundamentally transformed from the deflationary era, in our view. Globally, we have entered an age of geopolitical risk where supply chains can no longer be built on efficiency alone, making it likely that inflationary pressures will persist. While the expansion of AI may provide disinflationary pressure through productivity gains in the long term, in the near-to-medium term, we think the inflationary impact of global investment expansion is likely to prevail. If the government continues expansionary fiscal policy while implicitly applying the brakes to the BoJ, we expect upward pressure on inflation to persist, leading to continued upward pressure on long- term interest rates and weakness in the yen. The July rate hike was largely discounted but a more hawkish signal on rates will support the KRW, recognized as the most undervalue d currency on a 10 -year REER lookback (Figure 4). Finally, we maintain the long INR/IDR trade. Despite INR risks around higher oil prices (again), debt and equity flows to India have both recovered, as has real money INR flows (Figure 5). The fallout from rising oil prices seems contained for now. As for the IDR, while the threat of a sovereign ratings downgrade has diminished, a potential reclassif ication to ‘frontier market’ continues to weigh on Indonesia with a decision due in November. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW 4 USD seen softening despite rate hike calls: The USD has been strengthening versus the EUR since early May as expectations built for Fed rate hikes to come. However, we expect the USD to gently weaken versus the EUR from here, driven by our view that the continued delivery of fiscal stimulus in Europe should help improve European growth prospects and boost the euro – a trend we see as gold-supportive. US rates remain key risk: The fed fund futures market is currently pricing in one rate hike for 2026, but we note it has become notorious over the last two years for failing to correctly price US rate policy. We think mispricing risk remains elevated – and may be a significant upside risk to our gold price expectations – particularly given potential political pressure for rate cuts ahead of the November mid -term elections. We still believe in the investment case for gold: Once a convincing and durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is in sight, we think markets will switch focus back to various factors that we see as supportive for gold. These include US policy uncertainty, elevated geopolitical risks, slowing global growth, the fading appeal of US Treasuries and deteriorating fiscal outlooks in the US and Europe, as well as in developed Asia (among others) . 13/07/2026 Weaker USD, USD policy and economic uncertainty still look supportive Sources : Bloom berg, BNP Paribas forecasts Dav id Wilson, Head of Metals Strategy | BNP Parib

JPY The BoJ delivered a hawkish message alongside its June rate hike, yet another hike is still not fully priced by year end. Size of the wealth effect on consumer spending and its timeline: Conventional estimates of the ‘wealth effect’ coefficient range between 0.02 and 0.06. That is, for a USD100 increase in equity market and housing wealth, consumers spend somewhere between USD2 and USD6. Our modeling suggests a similar 0.05 coefficient over four quarters. This aligns with implied estimates from NiGEM, a large-scale macroeconomic model we’ve used in our work on tariffs, AI, and the Iran conflict (see Figure 7). Wealth effects not abnormal, but distributional differences suggest potential fragilities: Our breakdown suggests that while equity market gains have contributed more than usual to spending growth recently, the housing contribution is near zero, putting the net effect around 0.5pp – not unusually large relative to the past decade (see Figure 6). That said, the divergence between equities and housing is one way to illustrate the ‘k-shaped’ dynamic that commentators point to when referring to potential fragilities in the outlook. Equity holdings are concentrated among higher-income individuals, where the marginal propensity to consume tends to be lower, but the overall gains have been much stronger (see here). Looking ahead, we continue to look for a 50 -75k monthly pace, on average. We view such a run rate as sufficient to lower the unemployment rate by about 0.1pp/quarter given our breakeven estimate of 0-20k. To that end, the drop in the unemployment rate to 4.2% (matching our below-consensus expectation) was consistent with our view that the US does not need much in the way of jobs growth to keep the unemployment rate falling over time. We expect the jobs market to t ighten over the year, responding to resilient growth with a lag. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS The JPY Relationship. As highlighted in the Theme of the Week, a notable divergence has emerged within Asia FX. Despite being global technology and manufacturing powerhouses, TWD and KRW have traded more closely with JPY than with SGD or CNY. A closer look at trade structures helps explain why. Starting with export composition, Japan and Korea exhibit remarkably similar trade profiles and to a lesser extent Taiwan. Electronics and machinery dominate North Asia exports, but the overlap extends beyond technology. Transport equipment, chemicals, metals and plastics acco unt for a comparable share of exports in Japan and Korea, highlighting the degree of competition between the two economies (Figure 2). The similarity is more striking when examining export destinations. Japan, Korea and Taiwan all rely on a near -identical end- demand profile, with roughly 60% of exports destined for Asia, 23% for North America and 10% for Europe (Figure 3). By contrast, Singapore and China exhibit more differentiated trade patterns. Singapore's exports are overwhelmingly concentrated within Asia (72%), while China's demand base is more diversified across Europe and the broader EM complex. As a result, SGD and CNY tend to be less sensitive to JPY-driven competitive pressures than TWD and KRW. Resetting Asia. Our analysis suggests the threshold for slipping into a high-inflation regime from the current low-inflation regime has fallen to 4.7% and that there is less than a 15% chance of that switch happening as of Q1 2026. While the external pressures, especially from global commodity prices, have moderated, the RBI still needs to navigate new headwinds, and cross new rivers by feeling the stones, to ensure there is no policy slippage or error. Week ahead In the coming week, we turn our focus to the monetary policy meeting in Japan along with a flurry of data releases across the region. We expect BOJ to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.00% to gauge the impact of the June rate hike on financial conditions. With USDJPY at fresh highs of 163, we think the BoJ's objective going into this meeting is to firm up market pricing of further near-term hikes. On the data front, we expect China’s manufacturing PMI to come at 50.1 in July (vs 50.3 in June) on the back of moderated production activities. In Japan, we expect Japan-style core CPI inflation (ex fresh food) to edge higher to 1.7% yoy in July (vs 1.6% in June) due to higher energy prices. Meanwhile, we expect Japan’s IP to rise 2.0% mom sa in June (vs 0.1% in May) on higher production machinery, supported by firm AI-related SPE demand, while rebounds in general machinery and ICT products from low bases in May should provide additional lift. In Korea, we expect exports to grow 50.4% yoy in July (vs 70.7% in June) on one less working day compared to July last year but supported by a robust semi export. 24 July 2026 GEM Fixed Income Strategy & Economics Asia Table of Contents This Week in Focus 2 India

The fact that the final version retains the commitment to work closely with the BoJ toward price stability “without returning to deflation” suggests that the Takaichi administration's macroeconomic bias remains firmly rooted in continued reflation rather than inflation suppression. The revisions appear to be a reactive, defensive measure taken after the market’s negative response to what it perceived as an erosion of BoJ independence. While we expect the administration to concede to some acceleration in the pace of rate hikes given the yen’s persistent weakness, its underlying preference for low rates remains fundamentally unchanged, in our view. A change in risk management: This does not necessarily mean that the BoJ is currently “behind the curve”, as the central bank's position has been that underlying inflation has not yet reached 2%. However, the BoJ has now acknowledged “a risk of underlying CPI inflation deviating [to above] 2%”. This is tantamount to admitting that the policymakers are now facing a new phase and may arrive at a different conclusion when applying a risk management approach. In other words, while the central bank had previously seen the risk of premature rate hikes preventing sustained and stable 2% inflation as outweighing the risks associated with rate hikes being a little on the late side, the BoJ now appears to be less concerned about the risk of rate hikes cooling the economy and inflation than about the danger of sluggish rate hikes allowing underlying inflation to overshoot 2%. With underlying inflation now seen as at least approaching 2%, the BoJ should, in an ideal scenario, have already made more progress in normalising its policy rate towards ‘neutral’. In any case, there no longer seems to be any doubt that rate hikes should continue, and the only real question is the extent to which the pace of normalisation should be accelerated. E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 313/07/2026 The Domestic Liquidity Indicator (DLI) is a composite measure of overall monetary conditions in Singapore, published by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) in its monthly Statistical Appendix. Given Singapore’s status as a small, open economy managed via an exchange rate regime, the DLI is designed to capture the aggregate impact of both exchange rate and interest rate fluctuations, as the former influences monetary conditions through multiple transmission channels. Methodologically, the DLI is calculated as the sum of the weighted quarterly changes in the SGDNEER and short- run interest rates—proxied by the 3-month SORA rate— scaled by their respective estimated variances (for the original construction, refer to the MAS Quarterly Bulletin, June 2001). A positive value indicates a tightening of the monetary policy stance relative to the previous quarter, while a negative value indicates easing. Figure 5 presents our estimation of the DLI, including a decomposition of the weighted contributions from the SGDNEER and the 3-month SORA rate. records.text: and the economy continues to steadily recover. However, in a March updated report on the natural real rate of interest, the BoJ indicated that the lower estimates in its range (derived using time series models) are likely subject to a downward bias. Excluding those estimates leaves a range of –0.5% to 0.5%. Moreover, as the BoJ estimates the economy's potential growth rate at around 0.5–1.0%, it may be more appropriate for the central bank to assume that the natural real rate of interest is "non-negative“, implying that the neutral nominal rate is 2% (or slightly higher). The BoJ, therefore, may seek to raise the rate to 1.75% or 2% once it deems that underlying inflation has reached 2%. Appropriate policy rate when underlying inflation is approaching 2%: If the BoJ envisages a level of 1.75% when referring to “underlying CPI inflation (…) approaching 2%”, the appropriate level of the policy rate would be somewhere between 1.4% and 1.6% (or between 1.375% and 1.625% based on a strict application of our model). The 1.4% lower bound corresponds to a nominal neutral rate of 1.75%, while the 1.6% upper bound corresponds to a nominal neutral rate of 2%. In other words, the BoJ should, in theory, have hiked to around 1.5% if it believes underlying inflation is now within striking distance of 2%. records.text: hikes this year. Growth surprise is fading By no means is the U.S. economy signalling distress. However, the magnitude of positive economic surprises appears to be peaking, suggesting that much of the U.S. resilience story is already reflected in market expectations. Growth remains solid, but the moderation in upside surprises indicates the economy is no longer reaccelerating at a pace that consistently exceeds forecasts. This cooling in economic surprise data has coincided with a less hawkish tone from the Fed. Together, these developments suggest that, for now, the hawks have largely made their case. Unless either inflation or growth begins to surprise meaningfully to the upside, the market is unlikely to price a materially more hawkish policy path from here. The value of varying opinions Fed communication is back in the spotlight as Chairman Warsh seeks to reshape how the Fed communicates with markets. We track ia daily assessment of how the media interprets the tone of individual Fed officials. While the dispersion of member views has narrowed relative to the start of the Fed’s easing cycle, it remains higher than at the beginning of the year. Importantly, periods of greater divergence in Fed communication tend to coincide with increased volatility at the very front end of the yield curve. As a result, it is not just the number of Fed speeches that matters for markets, but the degree of disagreement in the messages being delivered. Risk on for so long Real money investors

El Niño events typically start to develop in May and peak in November/December before tapering off into next April/May. El Niño, especially a strong one, could fuel higher temperatures (and a milder winter) globally in H2 2026, as well as alter precipitation levels. We see risks not only for global energy and agriculture balances but also for key shipping routes, particularly against a backdrop of already tight global supply chains and lingering geopolitical risks in the Middle East. The market shock from El Niño is unlikely to be uniform, in our view, which could give rise to both risks and opportunities across equities. Our long–short equity trade idea aims to capture potential sector divergence: the long basket (BNPELNRL) focuses on El Niño adaptation and resilience beneficiaries, while the short leg (BNPELNRS) targets sectors vulnerable to weather-related disruption or demand weakness. records.text: : According to a study on ETF market development by a Chinese index provider, the total AUM of US active ETFs rose 74% y/y in 2025, accounting for >10% of total US ETF AUM (CSI, 27 February). There is also a trend for US mutual funds to convert into actively managed ETFs, which may also apply to the China onshore equity market given the intense competition on fund AUM. We think the rising popularity of active ETFs may bring more product differentiation, reducing the concentration of the AUM by issuers. Launched last May, active ETFs in Taiwan have become increasingly popular among retail investors over the past few months, with aggregate AUM rising from USD5bn to USD27bn since the start of the year, driven by both stellar market returns and sizable inflows into both current and new products. Given strong AI tailwinds, many investors have shifted toward active ETFs in search of excess alpha and outperformance relative to the benchmark index.

Higer commodity prices also lifted import values: iron ore and copper ore prices rose 6.8% and 38.4% y/y. respectively, driving the value of their imports up 9.2% and 27.2% y/y. However, oil import volume fell 30.3% y/y in Q2, after an 8.6% y/y increase in Q1. Tanker-tracking data shows the number of crude oil supertankers bound for China over the next 90 days did not experience a significant rebound even after the US–Iran memorandum of understanding was reached in mid-June. This suggests that China’s oil inventories remain ample and that the country is not in a hurry to procure additional supplies . China's trade surplus in Q2 rose modestly, up 0.6% y/y. However, import prices have been climbing much faster than export prices – export prices increased 9.0% in April and 14.2% in May y/y, while import prices surged 23.7% in April and 30.3% in May. As a result, the trade surplus in real terms continues to expand, making a decent positive contribution to GDP growth. Looking ahead to H2, we believe the resilience of China's export sector is sustainable. The AI-driven semiconductor super cycle appears set to persist, and China's strong competitiveness continues to fuel the export boom of auto and other products . records.text: onetary policy: Strong consumption, investment and trade data, expansionary fiscal policy and an expected surge in corporate capital expenditure suggest that South Korea’s GDP growth could be stronger than previously anticipated. We raise our forecast to 3.1% for 2026 from 2.7% previously and to 2.2% for 2027 from 1.9% (see South Korea: Growth forecasts revised up, CPI projections maintained, dated 2 July). Headline inflation posted 3.2% y/y (0.1% m/m) in June, compared with 3.1% y/y in May. Core inflation remained unchanged at 2.5% y/y, while living necessities inflation – a metric which the central bank appears to be monitoring closely – inched up to 3.4%. We see room for inflation to ease, thanks to lower global oil prices, but this does not mean that overall inflationary pressures will ease quickly, especially as the time lag could keep core inflation high. We still expect the Bank of Korea to deliver 25bp rate hikes in July and October 2026, raising the policy rate to 3.00% by end-2026. This would bring the rate into slightly restrictive territory, according to our estimates. We then see rates on hold for an extended period with risks tilted toward further hikes in 2027. Quaest polling indicates that, on average nationally, 26% of independents have no intention of voting, 40% would be willing to support Lula and 27% would back Bolsonaro. India: RBI update shows a strong start to Forex swap window On June 5, 2026, the RBI had taken a spate of measures aimed at boosting supply of foreign exchange and improving capital flows in the economy. The most prominent of these measures was the re-introduction of a swap window for foreign currency nonresident deposits raised by banks (FCNR (B)), along with removal of withholding and capital gains taxes on bonds issued by the government of India, and ECB issuances by banks. RBI's first release of information on foreign exchange swap window mobilization shows a strong start at USD20.7bn as of 17 July, roughly 6 weeks after the program was launched. This was primarily led by FCNR(B) deposits (USD17.4bn), with a further USD3.3bn raised through ECBs. The strong initial take-up has outpaced the 2013 scheme (in its first seven weeks or so had mobilized ~USD10bn), easing concerns about a weak response to the program and suggesting the RBI remains on track to mobilize USD60–70bn by the program's end. Sources: Kpler, Joint Organisations Data Initiative (JODI), Indian Ministry of Commerce & Industry, UNCTRAD, Macrobond, NiGEM, BNP Paribas APPENDIX Methodology: Our supply-chain risk index is made up of six indicators. Each is z-scored and normalised from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates the least risk of supply-chain pressure and 1 the most. Note that z-scores are computed across our sample of EM countries, rather than one country’s history. As such, a normalised z-score of 1, for example, means the raw data point stands the most standard deviations away from the EM sample mean, rather than the historical mean of that country. Intuitively, each country’s oil reserves over net imports and fertiliser trade balance are reverse-normalised (i.e. the higher these data are, the least risk to experience supply-chain pressure). We attribute equal weights to each indicator. Even a 57k rise in payrolls can trigger a decline in the unemployment rate , a s we saw in the June report. While increasing adoption of AI may help to somewhat address this labour market supply/demand imbalance in the future, this is unlikely to be a major driver of lower labour demand over the next couple of years when AI begins to complement current workers, rather than replace them. That may change further out, but we are not yet at the point where AI is replacing swatches of workers. We may get there in the future, and given the trends highlighted above , this may not be something to fear. We are just not there yet. Finally, the Fed (and thereby the market) reaction function to labour market data needs to change. As the supply of labour declines, we will see excess demand for labour rise, all other things bein g equal. That means potentially stronger wage growth in the future. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear Private pension provision is limited in France, amounting to 0.3% of GDP compared to about 0.7–0.8% in Itay and Germany, and more than 3% in the Netherlands and UK. It also represents just 2% of overall pension spending in France. There has been a pick-up since the 2019 launch of the Plan d'Epargne Retraite (PER), and we think growing interest in recent years may in part reflect public concern about pension system solvency. The PER hit EUR141bn at end-2025, and more than 12 million contracts, but remains well below the size of other savings channels like life insurance (EUR2trn) (Figure 6). We also note that detailed analysis from the Accounting Court shows that 60% of PER is in PERIN personal contracts, where wealthier savers make up the majority. Only 10% of ‘blue collar’ workers have a private pension versus 30–40% of ‘white collar’ workers. We therefore think a meaningful expansion of private pensions might require mandatory contributions to broaden take-up. Recent polls suggest this may be getting more likely. One conducted last year showed a clear majority (64%) of the public in support of private pensions (Elabe, September 2025) with a major swing among right-wing voters where support was at 70% or more. We think transition flows from the Dutch pension sector are likely to be larger than last year (see p.55 in Looking beyond the war, dated 11 May) while we see current positioning in speculative curve steepeners as significantly lower than last year. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. records.text: central banks sounding more, not less, hawkish. Valuation, FX flows, inflation resilience and central bank tone all favour the NZD. Long NZDCHF With the case for adding to NZD clear, the question is against what. CAD, CHF and GBP all appear in the Machine selections for different reasons. FX flows still show investors unwinding GBP shorts despite political uncertainty, so the Minds are sticking with the GBP long, unusual as that is for us. On CAD, as Noel Dixon argues here, the worst may be past. That leaves NZDCHF, neatly returning us to value: CHF is the most overvalued currency (Figure 2) and, partly as a result, has one of the most dovish-sounding central banks (Figure 4). Forest’s favourite trade this week, long NZDCHF, is therefore the first Machine selection added to the Minds’ weekly portfolio. And still USD neutral? Like the Minds, both Boost and Forest had been long USD in recent weeks but are now firmly neutral. That still seems right. USD support comes from relative growth, a still-hawkish Fed (Figure 4) and potential safe-haven demand from the Middle East conflict. Against that, the USD is expensive (Figure 2), FX flows remain negative (also Figure 2) and, as we warned in Rhyming regimes, troubling Sines, US data surprises were due a correction. The end result is similar to the quarterly update of our long-term relevance-based prediction model this week: higher conviction in USD inertia. In May when the market was initially concerned about a large supplementary budget, though ended up a modest one with JPY 3.1trn, swap sprtheead actually continued to richen. We think that two factors outweighed the cheapening factor from fiscal concern. One was the significant supply reduction for super-long end issues. Since the impact of supply reduction in 2025 was not so immediate, MoF continued to reduce supply for FY2026, likely resulted in an over-richening from 40y. Since swap spread is cheapest in super-long end, richening in that sector affected the whole curve. KEY MESSAGES We initiate a long 10s20s box trade. As swap spreads have not been a simply driven by fiscal issues, we prefer box expression than outright. Swap spread have generally richened since 2026 despite repeated fiscal events. We think extended supply reduction in superlong sector has impacted the swap spread across the curve, in addition to the banks’ change in their swap usage. Fiscal events can still affect swap spread as seen in the reaction over “Basic Fiscal Policy” from the end of June. But for the next month or so, we do not expect an important fiscal event. We like to use 10s20s box expression also to take 10s20s steepening in IRS. Trade idea: 10s20s box long. Target entry 26bp. Target exit 21bp. Stop out 20bp. Risk USD30k. records.text: 22 Global Economic Viewpoint | 23 July 2026 EM Strategy: cover El Niño under a hedge David Hauner, CFA >> Global EM FI/FX Strategist MLI (UK) El Niño + Warsh = caution We have been arguing to add hedges in summer for an autumn which may bring Fed hikes and negative risk seasonality, and El Niño adds to the negatives. However, trading El Niño in individual countries is tricky as many of the most affected markets have high carry, e.g. BRL, COP or EGP; in BRL and COP we see major rate cuts by 2027. Moreover, El Niño is likely to be materially impacting EM assets only if the USD is firm. Thus, our preferred hedge is long $/ZAR as a global proxy, and ZAR is highly affected by El Niño. Africa and LatAm most affected Our economics team finds inflation in Africa and LatAm to be most affected by El Niño. This is due to geography but also due to a high share of food in consumer baskets and stronger second round effects. Specific countries that stand out are Brazil, Colombia, Peru, Egypt and South Africa. records.text: ting threshold: the lagged value of targeted inflation (π t-1), so that when π t-1 ≤ τ the low-inflation sub-model is active, and when π t-1 > τ the high-inflation sub-model applies. The threshold τ is endogenously determined by a grid-search over the 30-th to 70-th percentiles of the sample inflation distribution (2000Q4 – 2026Q1). For each candidate τ we estimate the SETAR model and select the value that minimises the residual sum of squares while also achieving the lowest AIC/BIC. We re-estimate the model recursively in a 12-year rolling window to obtain a time-varying threshold that can capture shifts in inflation dynamics during episodes such as the GFC, COVID-19 and recent energy shocks. Markov switching models: We estimate a two-state, first-order Hamilton (1989) MS Phillips-curve that mirrors the reduced-form specification used in the SETAR exercise and further includes unit labour costs and the REER. The key distinction with the SETAR model lies in how the regime is modelled: the binary state variable Rₜ (high-inflation = H, low-inflation = L) is latent and follows a first-order Markov chain. Because the chain is first-order, only the most recent state influences the current transition – a “memoryless’’ structure that permits rapid, stochastic switches when new information (e.g. a supply shock or a credibility shock) arrives. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 23 July 2026 11 LatAm and EMEA usually most impacted Antonio Gabriel Global Economist BofAS We measure the impact of El Niño on macroeconomic variables with a Vector Autoregression framework. El Niño can impact inflation via food prices and second- round effects. Using a VAR, we find Colombia, Peru, and Brazil to be most exposed in LatAm, and Egypt and South Africa in EEMEA. In EM Asia, we find an impact on food prices, but not headline inflation. In the current context, a potentially severe El Nino is building on top of elevated fertilizer prices, and inflation risks could become yet again a headwind for monetary policy. A VAR approach We use a Vector Autoregression (VAR) to describe the dynamic relationships between El Niño and economic variables over time, including GDP, inflation, interest rates, and fluctuations in the real exchange rate. This allows to parse out the impact of El Nino from the impact of the evolution of other macroeconomic variables that should also impact prices and economic activity. Furthermore, this approach is useful to build Impulse Response Functions (IRFs) that evaluate the cumulative impact of how a given temperature shock may translate over time into macroeconomic variables. Retail sales suffer: As we expected, China’s overall retail sales rose just 1.3 % y/y in H1. After a 2.4% y/y gain in Q1, that indicated growth slowed to just 0.2% in Q2 alone . The deceleration reflects the waning impact of the consumer-goods trade-in program – for which subsidies were scaled back this year – combined with the steepest year-on-year base effect of the year in Q2. The discounts offered during the ‘618’ online shopping festival – a key driver of retail sales in May and June last year – also cooled off amid the anti-involution campaign . Above-scale companies saw sales of trade-in-subsidized goods (excluding autos) fall 3.2% y/y in Q2, versus a 30.3% rise in the same quarter last year. Auto sales plunged 15.9% y/y in Q2, hit by reduced subsidies and higher taxes on electric vehicles. Meanwhile, organic consumption momentum softened slightly, with sales that exclude subsidized items and jewelry expanding 2.0% y/y in Q2, down from a 4.6% increase in Q1. records.text: Lee Ferridge 13 July 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General US Labour Market: Rethink required US payrolls growth in June emerged weaker than expected and was accompanied by notable downward revisions to the prior two months. The reaction was as one would expect. The rates market reduced Fed hike expectations, pushing the first hike out to December from October and, subsequently, the dollar suffered. It is our contention that t his is the wrong interpretation of the report and, the market needs to rethink how it views US labour market data going forward. Due to labour supply constraints, the payrolls number is no longer a pure reflection of worker demand. Was the payrolls number lower because firms’ desire to recruit was weaker than expected or, was it because they could not find the workers required at the (current) price they are willing to pay? In other words, are low payrolls number a result of lower demand or lower supply? The former is a sign of lower growth, the latter is a sign of potentially higher inflation. Hence, the answer to this question is a key one for the Fed (and the market) to consider in the coming months. Shrinking The US labour force fell by 720k in June. Since its peak in November of 2025, it has declined by 2.2m or 1.3%. Excluding the Covid period, this is the largest peak to trough decline we have ever seen in the number of US workers. We see a few potential reasons for the relatively contained reaction thus far. First, the market could be assuming there is little incentive for either the US or Iran to return to full-scale hostilities that decisively bring to a close the talks initiated by the memorandum of understanding signed in mid-June. Second, the prevailing narrative of a post-conflict ‘supply glut’, as well as past experience of successful verbal intervention to cap prices, suggests that prices can remain rangebound unless and until physical shortages become more apparent. Third, the global economy has already proven resilient in the face of the higher energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty that greeted the start of the conflict in late-February. We broadly agree with this interpretation. Although risks have increased, w e don’t think recent events will significantly challenge the underlying resilience of the global economy, which remains supported by a combination of broadly accommodative financial conditions (at least in the US), supportive fiscal policy, and structural tailwinds from AI and higher defence spending. What’s more, although we see the cooling in US June CPI as an outlier rather than the beginning of a trend, it certainly appears to have diminished the perception that the Fed might need to act urgently. records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: AS YOU WERE IN H2, EURJPY What a difference a MOU makes. Oil prices have fallen sharply since the (fragile) Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran was agreed. While the MOU was actually signed on June 17th, the subsequent trajectory of oil had already become apparent in the days leading up. Not only is Brent now pretty much back to where it was when the conflict started at the end of February, but it is also 33% below its May peak. While official inflation data will take time to capture this turnaround we, of course, can turn to State Street PriceStats to see the impact in close to real time. That is captured in the final chart on the following page. Almost universally across the G10, inflation, as measured by PriceStats, is retreating (in some cases sharply) from its oil-induced peak. Canada, the UK and Australia are the most notable, with inflation in the latter now back below its level on February 27th. Some rates markets still need to catch-up. Some G10 rates markets have been quick to adjust to the post-MOU reality, others less so (Figure 4). Following the aforementioned decline in Canadian and UK PriceStats, we have seen BoC end of 2026 rate expectations fall from over three hikes to unchanged now (close to where they were prior to the start of the conflict). records.text: FOCUS F O C U S 13/07/2026 1 Following the pension reform law passed in March 2025, the Superintendencia de Pensiones issued a decree on 3 July 2026 outlining the new generational fund framework for pension funds. In this note, we explain the main changes that the new framework brings and the potential market implications, both in the short and long run. What are the main differences between the current and new regulatory regimes? The new regime marks a transition from a Multi-fund system to a Generational Fund framework. While the Multi-fund system allows contributors to select one of five funds manually, the new system allocates capital based on the member's birth year. This approach implements a ‘glide path,' where the investment strategy automatically becomes more conservative as the member ages. Every five years, the system rolls cohorts forward: a new initial fund is established for young workers, while the oldest intermediate fund merges into the subsequent, more conservative fund. This ensures that members move smoothly down the risk curve over time, rather than shifting between discrete A–E categories (see Figure 1). The new regime introduces a comprehensive performance evaluation and compensation framework. Currently, AFPs are benchmarked against their peers for the same fund type. However, we see two potential issues in the short term. First, it would not solve the imbalances in the pension system. According to estimates from the Accounting court, the tax deductions needed to incentivise increased pension savings over other tax-efficient products (Livret A, life insurance) leads to annual costs of around EUR2bn to the public finances. Second, higher private contributions would mean extra costs for firms and/or households during the partial transition from PAYG to a funded pension system. Financing PAYG already accounts for more than 17% of employee wages and 23% of employer wage bills, and we think overlapping contributions imply higher labour costs that could damage corporate competitiveness or reduce purchasing power for households at a time when rising inflation is re-emerging as a key concern (Figure 8). We also considered adding a second USD long to replace the USDSEK trade we took profit on this week. However, with the oil price receding to its Feb 27th level – a time when the market was pricing 2½ cuts from the Fed – we are wary. The improved labour market underpins the hawkish shift in Fed pricing and the risks from the upcoming payroll numbers are likely skewed against the USD. We do maintain our USDNOK long as the Fed remains the most hawkish central bank within the G10 but decline to double up on the dollar overweight given the aforementioned concerns. Estimates derived from macro data tend to find larger effects, while micro-level studies tend to find smaller or mixed effects across the population. For example, higher home prices unlock borrowing capacity for homeowners, but renters might spend less as they need to set aside funds for a more expensive future home purchase. Our sense is that estimates derived from macro data are useful in practice, even if the theory says that the underlying causal chain is more complicated. Wealth effects related to AI gains, combined with stimulus from monetary and fiscal policy and longer-term corporate optimism, appear important to explaining why the US economy has been resilient to shocks. The direct effects of AI gains in excess of broader market performance may have added 0.1-0.2pp per year to consumer spending growth (see Figure 8). records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: A LITTLE BIT OF NEARLY EVERYTHING Rethinking Commodity FX. Despite lower commodity prices, particularly oil, real money demand for commodity-linked currencies is showing signs of recovery. While the prospect of a supply glut would typically argue against exposure to commodity FX— especially oil-sensitive currencies—the FX market appears to be looking through those concerns. This may reflect growing confidence that oil prices have found a floor, with the pace of declines moderating in recent weeks (Figure 3). Although OPEC+ announced a further production increase of 188k bbl/day for August —the fifth consecutive monthly increase—uncertainty surrounding the durability of the Iran ceasefire clouds the supply outlook. With the MOU set to expire in late August, neither the recent increase in Strait of Hormuz traffic nor broader regional stability can be assumed to persist. Looking further ahead, governments are also likely to begin replenishing depleted strategic reserves later this year and into 2027. OECD inventories reportedly fell by nearly 163 million barrels between March and May, reaching their lowest levels since 1990. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve remains near its lowest level since 1983. Rebuilding these reserves creates additional demand and absorbs supply from the market over time, lending support to oil prices. As a result, we are reducing both our NOK and CAD short positions. records.text: About State Street PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of the prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. The interactive Country Inflation Series charts overlay against the relevant official measures of inflation, in all cases non-seasonally adjusted. Terms of trade: Elevated gold and metal prices have acted as a tailwind for the rand, and official ToT data show a material improvement since Q4 last year. records.text: 3 Insights SPOTLIGHT CHARTS Inflation alternatives Fed Chair Warsh has previously stated that he believes the Fed needs to adjust the way it thinks about inflation. More specifically, he has hinted that he would prefer a median or trimmed mean measure of inflation to be the benchmark, rather than core PCE. This topic is the focus of one of his five taskforces. That being the case, it is worth noting that in May while core PCE rose to 3.4% yoy, median PCE stood at 2.8% yoy and trimmed mean at 2.4%. If the inflation target is indeed adjusted later than year, it could have a meaningful impact on near to medium-term rate expectations. Working in the shadows pt 1 The other shift to the Fed’s operating model that Chair Warsh has stated he believes would be desirable is a change in its communications strategy. And, of course, there is a taskforce set up for that. More specifically, Warsh seems to want to end forward guidance. If this is indeed to case, then expect increased volatility. If we take the period of much-less forward guidance from 1993 to just before the financial crisis FX vol averaged 10.3. However, when the new RBI governor took office and his policies allowed for higher volatility in USDINR, the same spread widened to 100bp (Figure 2). RBI measures to impact NDS: We believe that the recent measures announced by RBI (see FX: RBI, BI try different paths to fight depreciation, dated 12 June 2026) – particularly on the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) and External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) fronts – will impact the NDS curve and compress the NDS to NDOIS spread in the following ways: 1. Before the RBI’s recent FX announcements, Indian corporates and banks used to borrow money from the offshore market using ECBs and paid NDS to hedge their FX risk. However, with the recent RBI measures, these borrowers will now hedge their FX risk with the RBI at a discounted cost, which will not impact the market. We expect USD15-20bn worth of ECB flows to be routed through this mechanism by the end of this year. This means that the paying flow from NDS will decrease significantly, resulting in a compression of the NDS to NDOIS spread. 2. We expect the measures announced by the RBI to generate USD70-80bn worth of inflows in total in the second half of this year. With higher headline reserves over the next 3-5 years, the RBI will have more ammunition to intervene in the FX market if needed. records.text: 1). KEY MESSAGES The Chilean pension system is transitioning from a 'Multi-fund' to a 'Generational Fund' framework. Under this new system, capital is allocated based on the member's birth year, with the investment strategy automatically becoming more conservative as the member ages. The new investment limits may limit AFPs' ability to accumulate local treasury instruments, potentially weighing down the BTPs. Nevertheless, as an aging contributor base adopts more conservative investment strategies, government bonds would be supported. We do not see a clear direct impact on the USDCLP or the CLP basis in the short term. However, if the aging of main contributors leads to a decrease in demand for foreign holdings, USD buying could shrink supporting the CLP and leading to a higher CLP basis. We expect minimal impact in the coming months due to the gradual implementation of the law and the fact that AFPs would be already broadly aligned with the new investment limits proposed by the new model.

records.text: ambitious fiscal expansion (see Not a speedboat but a supertanker, dated 26 May) sits against a wider backdrop that includes: political fragmentation limiting budget consolidation in France (see Fiscal challenges alongside growth resilience, dated 8 June); an atypically large pro-cyclical deficit in the US; uncertainty over potential new UK Prime Minister Andy Burham’s spending stance ; and rising government spending in Japan (see Analyzing potential government spending on investment plan, dated 26 June). Combined, these global fiscal considerations keep supply and term premia elevated at the long-end of the EUR curve and we see this continuing as a structural source of long-end volatility. • Uncertainty around AI impact: Our central case for the impact of AI is one of strong confidence and buoyant asset prices, alongside elevated consumption and investment growth. With demand initially growing faster than supply, we foresee strong labour demand and percolating inflationary pressures (see A hitchhiker’s guide to the macro impact of AI , dated 15 April). However, with the technology evolving rapidly, a stock market seemingly reliant on the theme, and a wide range of views on the eventual impacts of AI on the economy and inflation, there appears to be a wide distribution of potential outcomes. Terms of trade: Elevated gold and metal prices have acted as a tailwind for the rand, and official terms-of-trade (ToT) data have shown a material improvement since Q4 last year (Figure 5). Our estimates indicate that the ToT peak has passed with the reversal in metal prices. For the PLN, the ToT are improving alongside a normalising energy market. Balance of payments seasonality: Although the PLNZAR cross does not display a distinct seasonal pattern, there is some evidence that EURPLN trades bid into quarter-ends before reversing (see Seasonality roadmap 2026 update, 30 January). More-pronounced seasonality comes from South Africa: the income account drives flows because of substantial foreign ownership of domestic equities and bonds. Historically, Q3 (particularly end-July and end-August) tends to be a heavy coupon period (about ZAR100bn, followed by another ZAR20bn in September), with public equity dividends also concentrated in the quarter. Bloomberg estimates suggest roughly two-thirds of ex-dividend dates fall in Q3 in South Africa, amounting to a 1.4% yield for TOP40 companies (about USD18bn on an index market-cap basis). This seasonal effect is reflected in the BoP data and could begin to influence the rand, depending on the external environment (Figure 3). KEY MESSAGES Our positioning and valuation indicators su

We hosted a meeting this week with the President and CEO of Keytrade in Brazil, a leading global fertilizer trading company headquartered in Switzerland. 2026 is shaping up as the most abnormal and challenging year on record for Brazil's fertilizer market, driven by the convergence of geopolitical volatility, constrained credit access, negative barter ratios and weather-related shocks, making planning exceptionally difficult across the value chain. NPK deliveries are tracking to be down ~15% YoY in 2026 from 50mn tons in 2025, with potash posting a slight increase but nitrogen and phosphate seeing sharper declines. Consistent with this trend, Jan–Jun/26 imports show nitrogen down 15% and phosphate down 6% YoY, while potash rose 5%. The strait closure is manageable until it isn’t With formal closure of the Strait of Hormuz in early March, trade flows from the region ground to a halt. Thankfully, by that time, the Northern Hemisphere had largely sourced the product it needed for plant, while the Southern Hemisphere was out of the market. India, a major buyer of fertilizers, also went on a large purchasing spree in late 2025 which has set them ahead of the game for 2026. This seasonality ultimately drove a volatile price spike and correction in Nitrogen, while Phosphates continue to trade at near records (in part because sulfur cost inflation has been unrelenting). These bonds allow foreign investors to hold Indian local currency interest rate risk without navigating onshore restrictions, and banks handling these issuances receive NDS to hedge currency and rates risk, pushing NDS lower. ▪ Interest rate expectations also drive the NDS curve. As the NDS curve deviates further from the onshore Overnight Indexed Swaps (OIS) rates rates, arbitrageurs engage in relative-value trades to exploit the valuation differences. Because the RBI tightly regulates domestic derivatives, the offshore NDS market acts as a primary barometer and driver of currency sentiment. records.text: 1 Insights Classification: ComplimentaryMaterial ECB Preview: Hawkish Pricing Meets a Dovish Reality 21 July 2026 For markets, the ECB meeting this week is less about what happens on Thursday and more about what comes later this year—a path increasingly clouded by geopolitical developments. With just 1bp of tightening priced for this meeting and no updated staff projections, investors are far more focused on President Lagarde's tone and whether it validates the recent hawkish repricing driven by higher energy prices. ECB rate expectations have remained closely tied to oil prices, and as geopolitical tensions have intensified, pricing for additional tightening has risen sharply. On July 1, markets were pricing roughly 20bp of additional hikes by December; within the last three weeks that has more than doubled to 44bp, with investors now also assigning meaningful odds to a September hike. The media narrative has also shifted in a more hawkish direction (Figure 1), leaving markets focused on whether Lagarde will endorse or push back against the recent repricing. With commodity prices rising again, the focus has shifted back to inflation. While geopolitical developments have encouraged markets to look through June's benign inflation print, the breadth of disinflation—and in some cases outright deflation—suggests easing price pressures were not solely an energy story. Indeed, in the last policy meeting, RBI had delinked its FX policy from interest rates, but an environment where US rates are rising will create some challenges to circumvent. Third circuit: Should time lag determine policy choices? The third headwind for the RBI is managing these issues, especially from a temporal trade off, which exists between growth and inflation. The potential for growth is not particularly weak and for inflation to rise over the medium term appears reasonably high, and we believe the fine balancing act of setting policy for near term, but acknowledging the longer term risks, is what RBI could attempt in its upcoming meeting. As such, we see a hold, and messaging to emphasize risks on inflation management over the medium term, while waiting for clarity on growth in the near term.

records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear G10 FX | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY Symbol denotes our end-2026 outlook relative to market forwards We are moderating our bullish stance on the AUD as we think positive bottom-up drivers have faded. We previously argued that the key factors behind AUD outperformance were FX hedging by superannuation funds, wider rate differentials as the Reserve Bank of Australia hiked rates, and growing commodity trade flows. The case for all three is now less convincing. Superannuation funds trimmed their FX hedge ratios in Q1, and have even engaged in some active AUD selling into strength. Meanwhile, the scope for further rate differential widening to benefit AUDUSD may be capped by expectations for Fed rate hikes. And finally, growth expectations and trade balances have worsened amid recent global energy shock. As the AUD still provides an attractive yield, and given we expect global risk sentiment to hold up, we remain constructive. However, we do not expect the pace of gains seen in H1 to be repeated in H2 and are therefore less inclined to chase bouts of strength. Our intention now is to be more tactical and open-minded towards trading the AUD from both sides of the range (see AUD: Slower pace of gains in H2, dated 3 July). In June, headline CPI fell to 1.5% y/y, well below market consensus of 1.8% y/y. Our new CEE inflation profile does not see either headline or core CPI moving above the 2.5% and 3% levels, respectively, which should keep the CNB comfortable with an on-hold stance. We maintain our EURHUF forecast at 350 for year-end. Our bullish outlook for Hungarian assets continues to be driven by the narrative of euro adoption acting as an anchor for the forint (see Hungary: Euro Vision, dated 4 June). Unlocking EU funds remains the government’s immediate priority, in our view, as it expects to receive the full EUR10bn Resilience and Recovery Facility package (4% of GDP) by year end. In tandem with this prospective increase in EU funds from historically very low levels, we expect the domestic investment backdrop to improve, which should boost FDI. Together, we think these factors should more than offset any negative current account impact from the energy price shock driven by the Middle East conflict and keep the HUF supported. On the portfolio flow side, we see room for a meaningful pick-up in foreign inflows to local government bonds. We don’t expect underlying price pressures to subside quickly, so continue to see a final hike in September as more likely than not. According to our refreshed reflation risk framework, Thailand is the most vulnerable Asian economy to upside inflation surprises over the next year, with Mexico and the Czech Republic at greatest risk in Latam and CEEMEA, respectively – see EM: Reflation risks beyond the war, dated 3 July.

Election odds driving local assets: The key catalyst of local markets will remain the election outlook, in our view, with external drivers only amplifying or reducing the moves triggered by local politics. So far this year, USDBRL has been strongly correlated with the apparent probability of President Lula’s re-election, as market remains concerned about lingering fiscal risks in a status-quo scenario. After the rise of President Lula’s re-election probability, part of this negative sentiment around fiscal risks seem to be priced in. We note that the current election cycle has repeated the historical pattern of volatility increasing towards June in an election year (see Brazil: When elections spell volatility, 7 October 2025). This time, volatility picked up as soon as the market reduced the probability of a Bolsonaro victory around mid-May, with rates reaching over-sold levels and USDBRL moving up in tandem (Figure 6). Asymmetric outcomes: We continue to see an attractive asymmetry in rates heading into the election. Premium in the curves remains elevated, pointing to a bigger reaction in rates if investors see a route to fiscal consolidation bringing down the term premium. The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. For example, a multiple of 1 indicates that the current average spread is equal to the historical median spread for that currency pair, whereas a multiple reading of 2 indicates that the current average spread for that given currency pair is twice as wide as its historical median. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. It captures spikes in volatility in individual market components as well as correlation breakdowns – atypical co-movements – between these components. Consequently, we anticipate that excess liquidity will continue to keep SORA fixings at these low levels. USD rates beta: Although SORA fixing should remain low from a fundamental perspective, SORA rates exhibit high beta to global and US rates. With global central banks pivoting toward rate hikes in response to the recent energy-supply shock, and with regional fiscal balances deteriorating, Asian rates have traded with a paid and steepening bias, keeping the SORA curve steep. Compared with other Asian markets, front-end SORA offers one of the highest carry and roll-down (Figure 3). The recent uptick in rates driven by geopolitical tensions provides an attractive entry point to receive front-end SORA rates, in our view. Our base case assumes flows through the Strait of Hormuz will eventually normalize, despite short-term volatility (see Energy: Middle East oil and gas scenarios update, dated 24 June). The primary risks to this trade are a further escalation in the Middle East and a more hawkish Fed triggering a global sell-off in front-end rates. To mitigate against these outcomes, we are hedging the SORA receiver with a paid position in Dec/Mar FOMC expectations. Current pricing reflects only ~9bp of hikes, whereas our base case remains three back-to-back Fed hikes starting from Dec 2026. records.text: The recursive SETAR estimates show that the inflation threshold separating South Africa’s low- and high-inflation regimes has fallen – from about 6% in the early 2000s to roughly 4.7% in the most recent window (2014–26). This decline reflects lower headline inflation, stronger SARB credibility and the recent reduction of the target midpoint to 3% from 4.5%. In practice, a headline rate above 5% would now be viewed as a warning signal, versus being comfortably ‘low’ a decade ago. The two-state MS model confirms that once the economy enters the low-inflation state it is relatively sticky – the probability of remaining in the low-inflation regime in each quarter is 72%, implying an expected spell of 3–4 quarters. The high-inflation regime is less persistent, with a ‘stay-probability’ of 51% (or about a two-quarter expected duration). Our model puts the probability that Q1 2026 represented a high-inflation regime at just 14%. Together, the evidence suggests that the SARB now operates in a regime where the ‘inflation-is-a-problem’ threshold is lower. Notwithstanding a lower bar to enter a ‘high’ regime, our modelling yields encouraging results in that the economy is unlikely to flip back into a prolonged high-inflation episode. This is backed up by our own outlook for inflation discussed in the pages to follow. at minimises the residual sum of squares while also achieving the lowest AIC/BIC (i.e. the best combination of model fit and model simplicity). We re-estimate the model recursively in a 12-year rolling window to obtain a time-varying threshold that can capture shifts in inflation dynamics during episodes such as the 2007–2008 financial crisis, COVID-19 pandemic and recent energy shocks. Markov switching: We estimate a two-state, first-order Hamilton (1989) MS Phillips curve that mirrors the reduced-form specification used in the SETAR exercise and further includes unit labour costs and the real effective exchange rate (REER). The key distinction versus the SETAR model lies in how the regime is modelled: the binary state variable Rₜ (high-inflation = H, low-inflation = L) is latent and follows a first-order Markov chain. As the chain is first-order, only the most recent state influences the current transition – a ‘memoryless’ structure that allows rapid, stochastic switches when new information (e.g. a supply shock or credibility shock) arrives. Each regime carries its own set of coefficients (μᴴ, μᴸ), and the latent state is inferred via maximum-likelihood, yielding a regime-probability for each period. Inflation dynamics are modelled in a linear fashion in each regime. On 27 May, a series of 2x single-stock ETFs were introduced on the Korea Exchange, tracking the same two firms. The aggregate daily AUM of the 2x Samsung Electronics product and the 2x SK Hynix ETF have been at USD3.7bn and USD6.3bn respectively in the month since launch. Across both exchanges, the total AUM of Samsung and SK Hynix 2x single-stock ETFs represents 0.6% and 1.6% respectively of the firms’ market capitalizations. While 2x ETFs tracking broad indices (e.g. local benchmarks) and specific sectors (e.g. semiconductors) are well-established in North Asian markets, investors may take longer to adapt to the pricing dynamics and volatility of 2x single-stock ETFs, given their higher concentration compared with index/sector products. Considering the popularity of levered ETFs among retail investors in the US, we expect APAC investors to follow suit. While there could be new product launches, regulators could also tighten oversight of this product if they were to become more concerned about market stability, as suggested by recent comments from South Korea’s Financial Supervisory Service. records.text: Cayla Seder 8 July 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Information Classification: General Developed Markets Strategy Weekly : Ready, Set, Reset KEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Supply is priced. With the MOU in place, oil prices lower and peak hawkishness likely behind us, we are looking for a reset of sorts. In many respects, conditions have normalized relative to Q2, with oil prices returning to pre -conflict levels. Moreover, stronger-than-expected Middle Eastern exports raise the possibility of an oil surplus. OPEC+ has ratified the return of more than 900,000 barrels per day of production since the conflict began, although the full increase may not materialize. The group's cohesion is also being tested, with the UAE's departure in May and Iraq pushing for higher output. Both the removal of supply headwinds and new potential tailwinds have been priced for now, however, after crude prices experienced a -4 standard deviation move after the MOU announcement. Even with the risk of surplus increasing, Brent futures have been rangebound over the past seven trading sessions between $70 -$75/bbl. At the same time , oil-driven disinflation is now largely reflected in market expectations, leaving investors increasingly exposed to upside surprises. Furthermore, while incentives to restore normal traffic through the Strait are strong, tanker volumes have yet to fully recover, and periodic reports of vessels encountering disruptions should help place a floor under oil prices.

In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise the co sts associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline, as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich, and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real-time information on consumer behaviour. records.text: NP Paribas, Bloomberg As upside pressure in global rates and oil prices are affecting our Long Coltes Feb 2030 trade, we are reestructing the position to continue to keep exposure to the likely outperformance of the Coltes curve on the back of idiosyncratic factors. We are closing the outright long position and replacing it with a Long Coltes 2030 versus paying 4Y IBR. The change reflects the fact that EM curves are likely to continue to struggle amid uncertainty surrounding the Middle East conflict and the oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz. Despite external headwinds, we remain in the Coltes curve as there is a strong case for its outperformance in the coming months. In fact, the new government likely reducing issuance pressure in the short end/belly of the curve by extending issuance duration and by putting more emphasis on external sources (multilaterals and HC bonds) would allow the short end/belly to reconnect with fundamental drivers. Specifically, assuming a reduction of inflation expectations towards the 3.5-4% range, a neutral real policy rate of 4–4.5% (BanRep’s working assumption is 3–3.5%), and some reasonable premium, the 30s sector of the curve should trade closer to 10% rather than the current 12%. records.text: 1 Insights Classification: ComplimentaryMaterial The Dollar’s equity flow conundrum 14 July 2026 The dollar’s AI weakness? There has been much talk recently over the dollar’s vulnerability to any crack in the AI equity trade. But, is that really true? The argument runs that the AI trade has attracted huge amounts of foreign capital into the US and, given that these inflows are largely FX unhedged, should they subsequently leave as a result of any tech equity sell-off then the dollar would be vulnerable. On the surface this argument seems sound. Figure 1 uses data from the Treasury International Capital (TIC) report showing that over the last year net US equity purchases by overseas investors totals US$763bn, easily the highest on record. This now puts overseas equity inflows at close to those related to Fixed Income assets. Indeed, overseas flows into US Treasuries over the last year only total US$390bn, around half that seen into equities. Our own data shows that non-US real money investors have also embraced the AI trade in size (Figure 2), albeit not to the same historically relative degree as indicated by the TIC data. This implies that non-US hedge funds and retail investors have played a significant role in the US equity buying. When it comes to how FX hedged these flows are, there are no official numbers, but our own FX hedge ratio indicators should provide a guide.
