Thailand and Singapore are the most oil- intensive emerging markets, with oil consumption accounting for more than 10% of GDP in both. And among the four, Thailand is running lowest on oil reserves. South Korea imports more than half of its energy from the Middle East, while India, albeit less energy intensive, not only imports over 40% of its oil from the Middle East, but also gets around 35% from the same countries that supply China, mainly Russia. India is also vulnerable through fertiliser imports for rice. What has stopped a full-blown supply crisis so far? We think two key buffers have cushioned EMs from an energy supply crunch. First, the US (together with West Africa) has stepped up exports of crude petroleum products. China too has reinstated some of its product exports after placing restrictions at the onset of the crisis. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear Picking up the tab: Former PM and presidential hopeful Edouard Philippe has recently stressed that pensions should be at the heart of the debate between candidates (Politico, 5 July). We concur. Pensions spending in France accounts for more than 14% of GDP (Figure 9 on page 6). Among OECD countries, this is the second-highest ratio, behind Italy, despite the proportion of France’s population aged 65 and over being roughly equivalent to that in countries like Germany or Spain. Rising social security spending has been a significant contributor to the widening budget deficit in recent years, up 3.5% y/y over 2022–2024. Pension costs have been the most dynamic component in that, growing by more than 5% y/y over the same period following a rise in minimum pension levels and the automatic indexation to higher inflation (Figure 10). The 2023 pension reforms introduced a phased increase to the retirement age from 62 to 64 by 2030, but that was suspended last year, and the pension system remains in deficit (at an estimated 0.2% of GDP in 2025). Despite a baseline assumption from the COR of a resumption of the pension reform beyond 2027, the deficit is expected to widen to 0.4% of GDP over the next decade and reach 2.4% of GDP by 2070 – that is 1pp worse than the estimate it made just one year ago. Second, we expect the RBI measures to generate USD70–80bn worth of total inflows in the second half of this year. With higher headline reserves over the next 3– 5 years, the RBI will have more ammunition to intervene in the FX market if needed. This would reduce depreciation pressure on the currency, and many short INR positions will need to be unwound. As a result, we think this should bring relief to the forwards market and push the NDS curve lower, relative to the NDOIS curve. We also expect the realized volatility in USDINR to decrease, as the RBI can become active on both sides. If the USDINR exchange rate rises due to depreciation pressure, the RBI can sell dollars using the new flows to stop the move, and then buy dollars if the USDINR exchange rate falls to recoup the FX reserves lost in the last few quarters. With lower volatility, the premium in the NDS curve over the NDOIS curve should decrease, which we have observed historically during low-volatility environments. Finally, as local banks will be flush with INR liquidity once FCNR flows arrive, we think some banks may try to engage in USDINR B/S FX swaps to invest in US Treasuries, which may also push NDS lower. We exit our long PLNZAR trade idea at 4. 28 (−1.8% for a loss of USD180k), hitting our stop-loss after a dovish press conference on Thursday from NBP governor Adam Glapiński. Technicals had prompted the trade, with our positioning and valuation indicators showing stretched levels (see FX: Long PLNZAR on stretched technicals , dated 1 July). We also felt divergence between the Polish and South African central banks was well priced in. However, Glapinski has now clearly opened the door for a September rate cut and it was notable that he chose not to talk down the possible negative impact on the currency. We therefore no longer think 4.30 will remain a sticky level for EURPLN and believe the zloty may continue to underperform. After three consecutive years of PPI and export price deflation, they now forecast two consecutive years of inflation, with export prices rising 2.5% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027. Their numbers also embed a small appreciation in the RMB against the USD into year-end (6.70) and throughout next year too. This suggests that the value (price times volume) of China’s exports into the RoW is likely to further catch-up to still-resilient export volume performance (see page 3). We think China’s current reflation is sustainable. Re-running our NiGEM simulations shows that, on average, this will likely add 0.28bp to EM inflation through the next 18 months (all else equal), from a modest deflationary impulse of 0.21pp last year. Like before, the effects are likely to be stronger in those economies with the highest China-backward participation in their exports. A cumulative 4.5% rise in China export prices – 2.5% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027 – adds just above 0.4pp to EM Asia (ex India) inflation, on average, according to our modelling. It adds around 0.2pp to Latam and CEEMEA inflation, with Mexico (just above 0.3pp) and South Africa (just below 0.3pp) standing out. records.text: nsion reform law enacted in March 2025, the Superintendencia de Pensiones issued a decree on July 3, 2026, outlining the new regime for the pension funds. The corresponding new investment limits may exert downward pressure on BTPs, as AFPs' ability to increase their holdings of local treasury instruments is constrained. However, as contributors age and become more conservative in their investments, government bond demand is likely to increase in the long term, while foreign assets demand might drop. What are the primary differences between the current and the new regulatory regimes: The new regime marks a transition from a 'Multi-fund' system to a 'Generational Fund' framework. While the Multi-fund system allows contributors to manually select one of five funds, the new system allocates capital based on the member's birth year. This approach implements a 'Glidepath,' where the investment strategy automatically becomes more conservative as the member ages. Every five years, the system 'rolls' cohorts forward: a new initial fund is established for young workers, while the oldest intermediate fund merges into the subsequent, more conservative fund. This ensures that members move smoothly down the risk curve over time, rather than shifting between discrete A–E categories (see Figure 1). A fundamental difference for EM into the latest energy price shock was that FX performance had (for the most part) been remarkably well-behaved, however. EM FX positioning into the Middle East war was large, particularly for high-carry trades (the BRL, TRY and ZAR). We find that the initial unwind in FX positioning was on a par with the reaction to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, but we find it has recovered faster (currently neutral) than in 2022, when generally short positioning was sustained in EM FX as the conflict continued. We think part of this performance reflects a still firm market bias for a secular weaker USD (see Global flows: USD exposure set to fall, dated 15 April). We also think that, fundamentally, emerging markets are in a sounder position to weather the shock (see Macro: EM-DM divide is fading, dated 23 February) without compromising either hard-earned credibility gains around central bank inflation mandates or market optimism for milder, short-lived fiscal responses (page 9). records.text: till the goal: The Japanese government released on Tuesday its first ‘Basic Policy’ under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The document’s drafting process has followed an unusual trajectory, after JGB markets were rattled by an initial text deemed to suggest a potential threat to Bank of Japan independence. That section now includes a footnote intended to address those concerns, indicating to us the government accepts it cannot ignore intensifying market pressure. However, we do not see this as a major pivot in the Takaichi administration’s ‘high-pressure-economy’ strategy. Our fundamental view remains that fiscal policy will remain expansionary, and that the BoJ will face a degree of implicit pressure to maintain an accommodative monetary environment – even if the pace of rate hikes accelerates somewhat from here, as we expect. Correct diagnosis, wrong approach? The Basic Policy – an annual document which sets out a government’s fundamental framework ahead of the next budget formulation – presents a core diagnosis that looks sound, in our view. It calls for a more proactive government role to address major structural shifts in the international order and economy, such as changes in the security environment, technological innovation led by AI, and intensifying global competition in industry and technology. At a time when oil demand is historically around its peak, China’s step back from international energy markets helped EM better compete for imports. Although China’s 2026 oil demand has likely peaked, we think it will still have to refill its oil inventories via imports, given future energy-security considerations. The question is where from. Damage to energy infrastructure and residual uncertainty around transiting through Hormuz means flows from Middle East producers will be slow to resume (see page 6), which we think could push China towards alternative suppliers, such as Russia. Over the last decade, we find that China has also been importing more energy from Malaysia, Australia, Brazil and Canada. Emerging market nations who import energy from the same countries may face more supply-chain constraints and/or higher prices in the months ahead as a resumption in supply places a renewed ‘bid’ for energy products. We therefore include a measure of the similarity between the origin of EM energy imports and China’s to our quantitative assessment of EM supply-chain risk. This change means that up to 40% of the constituents can now be non-Hong-Kong-listed stocks, allowing investors to tap more into overseas companies. An ample Southbound investment quota, a lower NAV premium, and the flexibility of same-day trading all serve the needs of mainland investors who do not have the access to the QDII quota for overseas investments. ETFs holding non-HK listed stocks joined the ETF Connect in November 2025, starting with US equities. Those holding stocks from other markets such as Japan, South Korea and Australia entered in April 2026. records.text: e UK was likely to experience “further weakening in employment growth” as labour market conditions normalised following the anomalous post-pandemic period (see Eurozone & UK: Jobs markets on thin ice, but not cracking, dated 11 July 2025). In our view, this normalisation has now broadly played out and has helped alleviate domestic price pressures. That said, persistent noise surrounding data quality issues in the labour force survey has clouded the fundamentals, exacerbating concerns about the state of the labour market and complicating policy-making. Instead, we argue that the cooling in the labour market thus far has been gradual, orderly and is showing signs of stabilisation despite the energy-price shock resulting from the conflict in the Middle East. A slow churn back to normal: The decline in the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio (Figure 2) is the clearest sign that labour market conditions have cooled in the UK. The metric has steadily settled around long-term historical averages, primarily driven by the unwind of pandemic-era labour hoarding. These distortions and their subsequent unwind is visible in the Beveridge curve (Figure 3) as well as employee payrolls data (Figure 4). With regard to the former, the Beveridge curve has notably flattened since 2024, converging towards a similar slope to that seen over 2010–2019. records.text: E M – L O CA L E YE S F O R A G L O B A L V IEW 217/07/2026 The neutral nominal interest rate is the policy rate level that neither overheats nor cools the economy. It can be derived by adding the 2% inflation target to what is known as the ‘natural rate of real interest’. The BoJ has estimated the latter to be between –0.9% and +0.5%, implying a range of 1.1–2.5% for the neutral nominal rate with a midpoint of 1.8%.  is the policy reaction coefficient, measuring the amount by which the policy rate would be adjusted in response to a 1pp deviation in underlying inflation from the 2% target. Essentially, the larger the , the more aggressive the central bank's response to inflation. In the following discussion, we follow John Taylor's original framework by assuming  = 1.5. Appropriate policy rate for 2% underlying inflation: Applying this rule would result in a policy rate equal to the nominal neutral rate under a scenario where underlying inflation matches the 2% target. Therefore, when MIFOR go higher due to these corporate hedging flows, NDS also go higher. 2. When supranational agencies issue high-quality, INR-denominated bonds offshore (INR-Supras), it allows foreign investors to hold Indian local currency interest rate risk without navigating direct onshore restrictions. The banks handling the supra issuance on behalf of the agencies receive NDS to hedge the currency and rates risk, which pushes NDS lower. 3. Interest rate expectations also drive the NDS curve. Investors monitor the gap between NDS rates and onshore Overnight Indexed Swap (OIS) rates. When rate hike or cut expectations heavily skew one market, arbitrageurs engage in relative value trades to exploit the valuation differences. 4. The view on USDINR also impacts the NDS curve. A bearish or bullish view on the USDINR directly dictates NDS pricing by altering offshore demand, risk premiums, and speculative flows for INR. Because RBI tightly regulates domestic derivatives, the offshore NDS market acts as a primary barometer and driver of currency sentiment.

What else to highlight? The decree also addresses the derivatives limits in light of the shift to generational funds. Unlike the previous framework, where the Maximum Derivative Exposure Limit (LED) decreased from 3% to 2% for funds A-E, the new setup establishes a 3% LED limit for Generational Funds 1-5 (for individuals under 55) and a 2.5% limit for the remaining funds. This new setup is considered less restrictive than the previous one, as a larger proportion of age groups and derivatives balances under AFPs will be eligible for higher LED limits. However, in practical terms, we do not see a meaningful difference with the current situation, as we found losses under stress scenarios are still higher than the limit and potential unwinds mainly in foreign rate exposure rather than in the local Camara curve (see Chile: Implications of new limits on AFPs derivatives). Our worst-case scenario analysis, which assumes a 40bp parallel sell-off in rates, suggests that the aggregate net loss from domestic and foreign rate contracts could reach approximately 4.1% of total AUM (see Figure 9 and 10).

First, the wealth effect from a rise in equity prices have led to higher demand for housing. A Bank of Korea study found that realized gains from equity markets have been prioritized for property purchases, especially by non-homeowners (see in Korean , Bank of Korea , dated 7 May). It also found that the effect in South Korea tends to be weaker than that in other advanced economies such as US and Europe. Second, sharp rises in wages especially for certain sectors, notably the semiconductor industry, have led to increase in home purchases, especially in areas adjacent to the firms in those sectors. We think the government will continue to address such spikes in housing prices, potentially via higher taxes. The measures may include increased taxation for home purchases meant for investment purpose, for example, by cutting existing benefits in the current methodology. Despite such efforts, however, the surge in housing prices will be difficult to manage , in our view, due to strong demand, keeping authorities vigilant. GBPUSD is now close to its fair value after a recent rise in its spot, and USDCAD is now trading just within its upper fair value band. EURUSD meanwhile remains significantly cheap. In Asia, the model keeps its short USDINR position, with the pair’s fair value rising recently due to higher oil prices and stronger global equities. The model does not trigger any new signals. ▪ In CEEMEA, STEER closed its short EURHUF position for a loss of 1.6% after the cross reached stop-loss, while the model remains short USDILS with the pair remaining significantly rich. USDZAR meanwhile has converged with its fair value after appearing cheap. ▪ In Latam, the model closed its short USDBRL position for a return of 1% after the co-integration filter got turned off for the pair, reducing statistical confidence in convergence. The pair’s fair value has declined to 5.0007 due to higher commodity prices and stronger local equities. USDCOP meanwhile appears more than 3.5 z-scores cheap as at Friday’s market close, as its spot has continued to decline. The model keeps its long position on the pair. We expect the CLP to remain highly sensitive to broader USD fluctuations in the short term. Given our upside bias for the USD and US rates, we anticipate that USD strength will be most evident against low-yielding currencies, a category that includes the CLP. The CLP is likely to be kept under pressure, due to Chile’s central bank (BCCh) signal that no rate hikes are expected soon, the narrow interest-rate spread and low carry. The pressure will remain until hiking premiums return to the Chilean curve and the market ceases to use the CLP as a funding currency for FX carry trades. Looking over several months, we believe the CLP could regain its attractiveness, provided oil prices remain contained. A favorable terms-of-trade environment, potentially higher policy rates (offering better carry) and a recovery in domestic activity would all contribute to restoring the currency's appeal to investors, in our view. We consider outright is more monetizable than curve, as 5y5y IRS has moved about 90bp above the generally assumed fundamental level (long-term inflation [2%] plus real growth [0.5%].). The monetary policy outlook embeds our expectation for three rate hikes starting in December, via our expectations for the 2yr Treasury yield. The model does not incorporate the range of idiosyncratic factors we take into account in our short-term forecasts, which do not derive mechanically from this model. It does however incorporate the faster productivity growth we previously layered into our base case, emanating from AI, which means potential GDP growth in the vicinity of 2.5% through our forecast horizon. Key takeaways: Trend factors – namely potential growth, lagged spending, and the model’s constant term – can explain a lot. This aligns with the permanent income hypothesis of consumer spending, in which consumers tend to smooth their spending by borrowing and saving around short-term fluctuations, spending in line with their average expected income. Around that trend, short-term impulses can move the needle – faster wage growth after controlling for potential growth rates, gyrations in equity markets, tax policy and fiscal transfers. Real wage growth was negative in recent quarters, but we expect a reversal in H2 2026 as the job market has stabilized and headline inflation measures subside. Moreover, market expectations of US growth for 2026 have stabilized around 2.10% while 2027 forecasts are being revised higher, increasing 10bps in June to 2.10%. However, the magnitude of positive economic surprises is beginning to moderate. As growth data consistently exceeded expectations throughout Q2, markets responded by pricing in progressively more Fed tightening (Figure 4). A slowdown in upside surprises do es not necessarily signal economic weakness; rather, it suggests that economic forecasts have adjusted to the prevailing environment. As a result, fewer positive surprises may generate a more muted market response and reinforce expectations for only two additional rate hikes. Against this backdrop, even if there are signs the Fed is nearing peak hawkishness, we would be hesitant to fade higher front -end rates. The bottom line is this: policymakers will spare no effort to deliver a minimum 4.5% y/y growth this year, and they are ready to bridge that gap with policy measures, as they did consistently over 2023–2025. As such, we stick to a 4.6% growth forecast for this year and see balanced risks to our call. Mild reflation set to persist in H2: The GDP deflator rebounded to 1.5% y/y in Q2, putting an end to 12 consecutive quarter of deflation . PPI inflation rebounded sharply, climbing 3.6 % y/y in Q2 after a 0.6% decline in Q1. This PPI reflation was driven by a broad-based cost push, with prices for energy, chemicals, non-ferrous metals and the AI supply chain all jumping markedly. Meanwhile, CPI inflation moved up modestly, rising to 1.1 % y/y in Q2 from zero in 2025 after reaching 0.8% y/y in Q1. The uptick was not only driven by the surge in energy prices – core inflation has also firmed up a tad. This means that a low payrolls number may be explained as much by an inability to find the right peo ple to hire as it is a lack of demand for workers. In the near term, we think the BoK could consider a faster pace of rate hikes if inflationary pressures accelerate. However, if inflation gradually eases as expected, we think the BoK would prefer a quarterly rate hike pace. In the medium term, the implications to inflation from expansionary fiscal policy, ongoing wage negotiations and stronger growth pressures will matter , in our view . records.text: Marvin Loh Cayla Seder July 6 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Fund C onnect Q uarterly: A Hawkish Lead Into the Sec o nd Half The second half of 2026 is shaping up to be a pivotal period for cash investors. Markets are navigating a unique combination of cooling inflation pressures, resilient economic growth, a structurally hawkish Federal Reserve, and abundant system liquidity. While the Trump Administration’s agreement with Iran has reduced some geopolitical risks and eased immediate inflation concerns, Chairman Warsh’s Fed has maintained a firm policy stance, challenging expectations for an imminent shift toward easing. Against this backdrop, investors are reassessing the outlook for rates, liquidity, cash allocation, and the USD. In this update, we examine whether the Fed is approaching peak hawkishness, what markets are pricing for the path of policy, and how real-money investors are positioning for the months ahead. The final third of Q2 brought significant catalysts for change. First, the Trump Administration signed an MOU with Iran, marking a meaningful step toward reducing geopolitical uncertainty and inflation risks. Second, Chairman Warsh took over the helm of the Fed, ushering in a broad agenda for policy and institutional reform. records.text: Marvin Loh, Cayla Seder July 9, 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material FOMC Communications: The value of a word The FOMC communication process is getting a total makeover, drastically cutting expectations on future moves. Current Fed leadership views forward guidance as counterproductive for needed policy flexibility given the market’s view that such guidance should be seen as a veritable glide path. The distinct possibility now exists that the Fed reverts to a foregone era devoid of transparency into the process of debating inherent policy uncertainty. Warsh’s view that policy makers are hamstrung by their previous ly published views has merit. Yet, the unintended consequences of this change may have the effect of curtailing financial and real economy risk taking during periods of uncertain policy transmission. Historically, the Fed has increased transparency through communication when it believes the market may be less clear on how it aims to balance liquidity provision during transitory periods. In other words, any step too far in removing communications may do more harm than good. Bottom Line: Expect less Fed speak, shorter policy statements and limited economic projections which will likely increase financial market volatility. records.text: Dwyfor Evans 15 July 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material PLN and HUF: A Tale of Two Central European Currencies Poland and Hungary share many external influences, making relative monetary policy, political developments and interest rate differentials key drivers of the PLN/HUF cross-rate. Recent downside inflation surprises in both economies have shifted attention towards prospective rate easing. While markets have become more optimistic about disinflation, they remain sceptical of a meaningful NBP easing cycle. By contrast, Hungarian rates have repriced significantly, pricing around 50bps of MNB cuts over the next 1 2 months. Despite this narrowing in expected rate differentials, the HUF has remained resilient. Hungary's April election and prospects for EU -related inflows have helped offset a less supportive rates backdrop. At the same time, carry has re -emerged as a dominant investment theme, driving strong real money inflows into high -yielding currencies such as the HUF. Positioning and fixed -income hedge-ratio indicators reinforce this preference, with investors maintaining outright long HUF exposure. The case for s hort PLN/HUF therefore remains supported by carry, flows and post-election optimism, but increasingly crowded positioning warrants greater caution. Policy divergence drives currency divergence: Poland and Hungary are exposed to many of the same external factors by dint of geography and economic linkage

While progress may not be smooth, we still expect talks to continue and kinetic action to recede (even if unevenly). That should prevent dramatic price upside – and perhaps encourage some downside assuming tensions ease again. However, we think recent events are likely to constrain flows out of (and particularly into) the strait as they have spotlighted elevated levels of uncertainty and risk – with contradictory messaging about whether the strait is open or closed a case in point. This likely lengthens the timeline for a normalisation of flows through Hormuz. As crude prices remain highly responsive to macro headlines and an expected supply glut, we still see upside as limited, even factoring in the sharp correction lower from the April peaks and further moderation towards pre-war levels since the 17 June signing of the US–Iran memorandum of understanding. This reflects a rebuilding of term premia driven by higher bond supply, the potential for fiscal and headline risks to materialise, and a likely intensification of political risks into 2027 as key elections approach. This outlook is further reinforced by the lack of visibility regarding AI’s impact on the neutral rate and a global environment of significant fiscal deficits, which keep long- end supply and term premia elevated. Curve steepening: We expect EUR curves to continue to steepen this year. As 2027 approaches, markets may begin pricing in rate cuts, while the ongoing Dutch pension fund transition and term premia rebuilding could add further steepening pressure. Spreads: Given our expectation for ECB hikes and market volatility, we think EGB spreads will widen into Q3 led by France, as budget discussions rekindle deficit concerns. We see elevated political uncertainty linked to 2027 elections in France, Italy and Spain. By Q4 2027, spreads would be likely to tighten again if the new governments pursue fiscal consolidation. records.text: 2 Global Economic Viewpoint | 23 July 2026 A severe El Niño is likely emerging Daryna Kovalska Commodity Strategist MLI (UK) Antonio Gabriel Global Economist BofAS Pedro Diaz Caribbean Economist BofAS El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a natural phenomenon that leads to changes in temperature in the Pacific, causing higher average temperatures worldwide. El Niño episodes typically last between nine and 12 months, tend to develop between March and June, peak between December and April, and start weakening between May and July. In contrast, periods of lower temperatures give rise to La Niña, which is more persistent. The Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) measures the average sea surface temperatures across the equatorial Pacific Ocean. El Niño is defined by periods when ONI temperature levels are more than 0.5 degrees Celsius above normal, while the opposite defines La Niña. Exhibit 1 shows a long-term time series of ONI, including past episodes of both El Niño and La Niña. Temperatures are already above average since the beginning of the year, and experts have been warning about a high likelihood of a severe El Niño developing. Since the beginning of the year, sea surface temperatures have been above average, with ONI crossing the 0.5°C threshold in April and reaching 1°C in May. Severe El Niño episodes tend to reach peak temperatures at over 1.5-2°C above average, and forecasting models point to a high likelihood of a severe episode ahead (Exhibit 2 & Exhibit 3). This looks out of kilter with the message the ECB is actually sending. BoJ still underpriced? Japan is the exception here. records.text: 10 Large discrepancies between pollsters: In the 2006 elections, only three major institutes – CNT, Datafolha and Ipope – published polls of voter intentions for the presidential race. From the 2010 elections, Vox Populi, and CNI had joined this group. In 2022, the field became more crowded, with 14 pollsters gauging how Brazilians would vote for president. With that context, we examine 12 polls that consistently released data throughout the 2022 election, aiming to assess their accuracy against the final results. In the first round, the two front-runners were generally mis-estimated, especially Jair Bolsonaro, whose support was repeatedly underestimated: his vote share in opinion polls was, on average, 3.6pp lower than the actual result. The largest discrepancies came from Ipes​p, Quaest, and Datafolha, each undershooting Bolsonaro by about 7–8 pp. CNT and PoderData were the most accurate overall. In the second round, CNT again proved the most reliable, only 0.2pp off Lula’s winning vote share, followed closely by Paraná and Quaest (0.5pp and 0.8pp, respectively; see Figure 10). Samples can make the difference: We observe variations in virtually every characteristic of the samples — gender, age, region, and education (see Figures 11– 14 overleaf) – which is likely to bias a particular pollster’s results depending on the dominant traits of the surveyed population. Due to the structural complexity of these technologies, demand for tester equipment remained strong, while demand for standard mass-production-line equipment was stagnant. In July 2025, Tokyo Electron reported that short-term demand for equipment would fall short of expectations, citing: (i) reduced legacy investment by Chinese manufacturers; (ii) revised investment plans by certain advanced-logic customers; (iii) cautious spending by customers of NAND storage; and (iv) reduced equipment need, resulting from yield improvements by HBM (high bandwidth memory) manufacturers. In early 2026, equipment makers indicated limited market expansion in H1 due to supply-side constraints, including insufficient cleanroom capacity. The real cycle begins now: At present, however, all last year’s constraints appear to be improving. Major semiconductor manufacturers have disclosed expanded capex programs. Memory manufacturers, previously focused on long-term customer contracts, are now articulating capacity-expansion plans. First circuit: Prioritize growth or prioritize inflation? The first issue that we believe needs to be determined is whether RBI should prioritize growth, or should it be concerned about inflation? Indeed, since the previous policy meeting, commodity prices have declined, rupee has modestly appreciated, and growth indicators appear resilient. Still, inflation passthrough, especially considering the prospects of a weaker monsoon and higher fuel costs, needs to be navigated as well. For now, we believe RBI will be slightly more driven by growth concerns given re-escalation of tensions in West Asia, but inflation too is quite important in the policy framework. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 217/07/2026 To understand how changing conditions affect South Africa’s Phillips curve (i.e. its state dependency), we replicate the approach used by the SARB in a June 2025 working paper. That study used two complementary tools: a Self-Exciting Threshold Autoregressive (SETAR) model and a two-state Markov-switching (MS) model. This framework is intended to identify both the inflation threshold at which the economy switches regimes and the persistence of each regime once entered, thereby capturing the state-dependent dynamics of inflation. SETAR: We estimate a reduced-form Phillips curve (lags of inflation, 2y inflation expectations, output gap) in which inflation dynamics can move between a ‘low-inflation’ and ‘high-inflation’ regime based on a ‘self-exciting’ threshold. That uses the lagged value of targeted inflation (π t-1), so that when π t-1 ≤ τ the low-inflation sub-model is active, and when π t-1 > τ the high-inflation sub-model applies. The threshold τ is endogenously determined by a grid-search over the 30th to 70th percentiles of the sample inflation distribution (Q4 2000–Q1 2026). For each candidate τ we estimate the SETAR model and select the value that minimises the residual sum of squares while also achieving the lowest AIC/BIC (i.e. the best combination of model fit and model simplicity). Performance is evaluated against this benchmark using tracking error, the information ratio, and returns in rolling 36-month windows. If an AFP’s performance exceeds the reference portfolio beyond a specified tolerance band, it earns an additional fee. Conversely, underperformance below the tolerance band requires the AFP to compensate the fund from its own capital. Performance within the band triggers neither reward nor penalty. Furthermore, the generational regime applies allocation ceilings for growth versus protective assets, as well as FX hedging requirements, based on the member's lifecycle stage. This more granular design is consistent with the ‘glide path’ concept and explicitly formalises categories for alternative assets, such as private equity. What is the expected timeline for the implementation of the new regime? Following the publication of the pension reform law (Law 21.735) on 26 March 2025, the finalised investment regime for generational funds had to be issued within 18 months, setting a deadline of September 2026. records.text: Singapore continues to benefit from the AI supercycle as a well-positioned trading hub in Asia. The latest NODX (non-oil domestic exports) print in May was higher than expected at 38.4% y/y (consensus expectation: 30.5%), driven by strong electronics exports. Domestic demand also continues to be upbeat, though its momentum shows some signs of moderation – May retail sales (3% y/y) and industrial production (13% y/y) data both came in lower than expected and weaker relative to the prior month. Inflation is well managed – headline and core CPI growth remain benign at 1.8% and 1.4% y/y respectively, as energy and services-related prices eased. With many components of the CPI basket subsidised or subject to price controls, and ample fiscal revenues to maintain these measures, inflationary impulses should remain contained. In turn, we see little need for the MAS to raise the SGDNEER slope further. USDMYR rose sharply in June amid broad USD strength and rising political risks following snap elections in the states of Johor and Negeri Sembilan. The Johor election resulted in a stronger outcome for the Barisan Nasional party, as expected, which reaffirms the risk of tensions among the governing coalition partners (BN is currently one of the partners). However, markets appear to have embedded a political risk premium. KEY MESSAGES • Our base case remains that the US Federal Reserve will hike rates in December, with risks skewed to earlier. • Consistent with this we remain long USDs and paid the front end in the US as we think the market is under-pricing the number of hikes this cycle. • We continue to expect a final ECB rate hike in September. Our call is for a December hike by the US Federal Reserve, and the latest nonfarm payroll print leaves us comfortable with that, although we continue to see risks skewed towards an earlier move. Our framework for a hike is the unemployment rate hitting 4.0% or signs of inflationary entrenchment into long-term expectations (see US June jobs: Staying onside , dated 2 July) Both these tests remain on track to be satisfied by year end. The unemployment rate is falling, and US Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s effort to realign inflation expectations and resolve the persistent problem in core inflation with tough talk will, in our view, require action in order to be credible. Raising rates earlier could reinforce Warsh’s inflation bona fides and support the notion of regime change. But a move in Jul y, for example, would be deeply divisive at the Fed, with likely dissents from Williams and Paulson and perhaps

cal revenue. Even in such a case, the available USD for FX intervention does not fall. This is because when the ‘surplus’ is transferred to the budget, the FX reserve account does not sell the USD as selling dollars would be considered an ‘intervention’. Instead, F-bills (JPY) are issued and the proceeds are transferred to the budget (Figure 5). Regardless of the status of the strategic investment, we think the USD/JPY xccy basis will continue to tighten. One of our arguments for this is that Japanese banks’ USD funding position looks quite comfortable. As Figure 6 shows, the amount Japanese banks need to fund in the wholesale market (= loan less deposit) remains small, while the total loan value has increased over the past year. To capture the potential 5s10s dis-inversion and overall tightening of USD/JPY xccy basis, we like the paid 5y5y. If the 5s10s dis-inverts and becomes flat the 5y5y, USD/JPY xccy basis can tighten by 8~9bp, excluding the change in outright level. Over the last month, the tightening trend has reversed somewhat, likely due to the correction in risk-asset prices (Figure 7), so the trade offers a relatively attractive entry. We initiate this trade idea by taking account of the market concerns about a further correction in risk asset, as the xccy basis has repeatedly tightened more after widening (Figure 8). Equity ETFs make up 55%, bond ETFs 18%, and the remaining 26% comprises commodity, money-market, and cross-border products. While we remain constructive on AUD, we think this requires a further rally in global equities, and we do not expect the same pace of gains in H2 compared to H1. The bullish bottom-up outlook for AUD was predicated on three key drivers: greater Australian superannuation fund FX hedging; wider rate differentials on Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes; and growing commodity trade flows. The case for all three is now less convincing, in our view. First, superannuation funds reduced FX hedge ratios by a small amount in Q1 2026 – the APRA data shows some active AUD selling into strength by superannuation funds (see Figure 1 and Figure 2). Second, the scope for further rate differential widening may be capped by future Fed rate hikes; third, growth expectations and trade balances have worsened amid the recent energy shock (see Figure 4 and 5, page 2). Since the number of Fed speeches troughed in 2012, we can attribute the upswing to the enhanced communication strategy implemented that year. Having said that, after an initial surge , overall Fed speak was generally stable leading up to the pandemic. Only after starting the rate hiking cycle did we see a notable uptick in in the amount of Fed speak. Concurrently, overall policy has undergone the biggest shift since the GFC during this period, with the most aggressive hiking cycle sin ce the Volker years. records.text: Ben Luk 2 July 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General EM Inf lation in Focu s : Worst is Over and It Was Never That Bad What Oil Shock? The combination of an oil supply shock and a rise in inflation expectations have once again tested EM, forcing central banks to hike—both to anchor inflation and to defend currencies amid a stronger USD and higher U.S. yields. EM fuel inflation behaved as expected, rising sharply from ~5% yoy pre-conflict to ~20% by mid-June. However, the pass- through to broader prices has been limited. Unlike the 2022 Russia –Ukraine shock—when elevated fuel prices coincided with surging food inflation and pronounced EM FX weakness —this cycle looks materially d ifferent. Two key buffers stand out: (1) FX resilience - Aggregate EM FX has depreciated only ~2.5% vs. USD over the past four months, containing imported inflation. (2) Benign food prices - EM food inflation eased from 6.1%yoy pre-conflict to 4.7% by June, reducing pressure on headline CPI given its large basket weight. As a result, despite the energy shock, aggregate EM inflation dynamics—and by extension growth risks—have remained far more contained than in prior cycles and the worst looks to be over. LatAm. Disinflation momentum remains intact across LatAm despite the oil shock. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear Working relationships: In light of the French public’s opposition to increasing the retirement age, proposals have emerged that instead link pension benefits solely to the number of years worked. This has primarily been advanced by former PM Gabriel Attal, and hinted at by RN’s Bardella. This would offer greater flexibility in how French workers decide their retirement plans, but we think past experience suggests it may be less effective in reducing financial imbalances in the pension system for two main reasons. First, raising the retirement age (i.e. making employees work longer) is seen as having a more significant and rapid impact. One estimate (IFRAP/CNAV, 23 June) indicates that increasing the retirement age by one extra year (to 65 for those who started working at 20), could reduce the pension deficit by between EUR23–27bn per year over the medium term. However, increasing by two the number of working years required to receive full pension benefits (to 45 years), for the same cohort, would yield a benefit of just EUR17–20bn (Figure 3). Second, increasing the retirement age appears to be a more effective way to boost the participation rate. According to the Accounting Court, pension costs would be more than 1pp of GDP lower if the participation rate among seniors in France (61.7% for 55–64-year-olds in 2025) was similar to that in Germany (75.4%). records.text: Raising the retirement age: Following various pension reforms since 2010*, the retirement age has increased by 2.5 years, reaching slightly more than 63 years in 2025. The pension reform (if reinstated from January 2028) is expected to contribute to a further increase in the retirement age to 64.5 years over the long term. However, according to COR estimates, rebalancing the system would require raising the retirement age to 65 years old in the next decade and up to 67 years old over the long term. - Cutting pension benefits: Pension spending accounts for more than 14% of GDP (over 24% of total spending). This ratio is expected to remain relatively stable over the next decade but then increase to 15.3% by 2070. This expected stabilization is due to the assumption that pension benefits will be indexed to inflation but not to productivity (expected to grow by 0.7% year-over-year). Unless a stronger productivity trend is assumed, rebalancing the system would require further adjustments to pension benefits, fueling the debate on not fully indexing pensions to inflation. We estimate that pensioners would need to accept a loss of purchasing power of around 4% per decade to rebalance the system (Figure 11). - Increasing taxes: The COR has estimated the impact of increasing employee or employer contributions to the pension system. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 203/07/2026 At the start of 2026, media reports pointed to increased USD FX hedging by three of the 10 largest Australian superannuation funds (see: FX: Superannuation flows – from bearish to bullish AUD, dated 27 January). Q4 2025 APRA data showed that superannuation fund FX hedge ratios on foreign equity holdings had risen to 23.6% by end-2025, from a low of 19.6% in Q3 2024. However, the Q1 2026 data, released last week, showed a pause in this rise in FX hedge ratios, with a small decline of 0.5pp from 23.6% to 23.1%. That can be explained by FX-un-hedged foreign equity holdings falling more than FX-hedged foreign equity holdings, in proportional terms. The AUD rallied in Q1, implying that, all else equal, FX hedge ratios should have risen. The small decline therefore suggests superannuation funds actively sold AUD into strength in Q1 thereby preventing FX hedge ratios from rising (see Figure 1). We estimate this selling amounted to AUD9.8bn, which points to a change of behaviour from Q3 and Q4 2025, when we estimate superannuation funds bought AUD7.9bn and AUD22.3bn respectively, while the AUD rallied (see Figure 2). The Q1 figure is only one data point pointing to a pause in the rise in FX hedge ratios. However, we do think future data releases would need to demonstrate FX hedge ratios were back on the rise for this theme to be a source of support for AUD

Our forecast is conditioned on gradual tightening in the labor market, job gains in the 50-75k range, a rebound in inflation-adjusted wage growth, historically moderate gains in equity markets and home prices, and a gradual pickup in labor productivity derived from our work on AI. Fundamentals, not vibes: Astute readers will notice we don’t mention consumer sentiment. We acknowledge the disconnect between sour consumer moods and higher levels of spending, but the bottom line is that the conventional sentiment indicators tell us little about future spending that is not already explained by fundamentals; a finding consistent with US Fed research (see here). Index construction and consumers’ perception of inflation or affordability help to explain the gap. The remainder likely comes down to an ageing population, political partisanship, and perhaps the increasing ease with which individuals can compare themselves with others, usually unfavorably, on social media. Source: Bloomberg, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Fig. 1: Spread between 3y NDS and NDOIS has widened The Indian rupee non-deliverable forward (NDF) and swaps (NDS) market is one of the largest NDF markets in the world. It exists because the INR remains only partially convertible, in that onshore forward access requires documented underlying exposure and approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Therefore, international investors often use the NDF/NDS market to express their views on INR movements. What flows drive the NDS market? The NDS market is highly flow-driven, especially in the 3–10y part of the curve, with the main flows as follows: ▪ Indian corporates and banks that raise money abroad typically pay Mumbai Interbank Forward Offer Rate (MIFOR) swaps to hedge their forward USDINR risk and meet their USD needs when the bonds or loans mature. The MIFOR and NDS markets in India are highly correlated because they reflect the same underlying economic variables – the interest rate differential between India and US rates, and the perceived future value of the INR. Therefore, when the MIFOR goes higher due to these corporate hedging flows, so do NDS rates. ▪ Supran

records.text: Ning Sun 15 July 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Colombia: Room for the rally to continue Recommendation: We recommend re-establishing a short USDCOP position, supported by our recent Colombia visit and internal positioning data. We had taken profit ahead of the June runoff to manage election risk, but de la Espriella’s victory has extended Colombia’s EM asset outperformance. The lack of post-election profit-taking has raised questions over whether the COP rally has become stretched and vulnerable to a near-term reversal. To address these concerns, we spent last week in Colombia meeting with the central bank as well as a broad range of local investors. Our discussions reinforced the view that BanRep is likely to maintain a hawkish policy stance for longer than markets currently expect (Figure 1). The State Street PriceStats series continues to indicate that monthly inflation remains well above the 3% annualized target (Figure 2). The BanRep board remains focused on ensuring inflation converges sustainably toward target and appears unwilling to make optimistic assumptions about the fiscal outlook despite the sharp improvement in market sentiment. Officials emphasized that they prefer to wait for concrete fiscal measures from the incoming administration rather than extrapolate from recent rallies in local bonds and CDS. Importantly, the central bank appears comfortable with a stronger peso, recognizing its role in helping lower inflation and attract capital.

records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General US has declined over the last year. After peaking at 32.2mn in March 2025, the number now stands at 30.7m, a decline of 1.5mn or close to 5%. Figure 4 No longer rising Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg Put these two trends together and you end up with a declining workforce, as illustrated in Figure 2 . Over the last twelve months the domestic born US workforce has declined by 0.5% while the number of US workers born overseas has fallen by 1.5%. These trends are not going to change anytime soon and so, unlike in 2013, the decline in the US workforce in 2026 is very unlikely to prove a temporary phenomenon. This is a trend that is here to stay. The participation myth Despite the data presented above, there are those who argue that the decline in the workforce is due to reduced participation rates and hence, conclude that these workers could soon return to the labour market. For sure, the adult participation rate is now at 61.5%, its lowest reading since February 2021 when the Covid impact on the labour market was still being felt. However, adult participation rates have been in a long-term downtrend since 2000. Why? Because a larger and larger share of the population is now retired. And that trend is merely going to accelerate. To get a truer picture of participation rates , we need to look at the participation rate of those in their prime working years (25- 54), and this tells a very different story (Figure 5). EM BOND WATCH China’s latest inflation rebound Figure 6 Disinflationary (for now) China’s recent rebound in headline CPI appears to be driven primarily by supply -side factors rather than a meaningful improvement in domestic demand. Producer prices have recovered significantly in recent months, largely reflecting the surge in energy prices and higher upstream input costs. At the same time, June credit data continued to point to weak underlying demand conditions, with overall loan growth remaining subdued. Notably, household loans have contracted for four consecutive months, suggesting tha t household deleveraging is far from over. Against this backdrop, rising energy costs are unlikely to support a sustainable recovery. Instead, higher input prices act as a tax on businesses and consumers, eroding purchasing power and profit margins, and po tentially weighing further on China’s already fragile demand recovery. The ECB’s July meeting delivered a hawkish tone that suggests the Governing Council remains squarely focussed on inflation risks (see ECB: A game of two halves, dated 23 July) . This hawkishness came despite ECB President Christine Lagarde noting that energy prices were close to the central bank’s June ‘baseline’, that the ECB does not see evidence of second -round effects and that it believes inflation expectations are well anchored (for now) . We interpret this in a few ways. First, the ECB is not overly concerned about growth – and the strength of Friday’s PMI data supports its view here. Second, it once again highlights the ECB’s sensitivity to the level of energy prices. The more elevated e nergy prices are, the lower the degree of evidence required on second -round effects to justify further tightening, in our view. Third, the ECB is probably comfortable with the market pricing in several more hikes , in that it helps to lean against second -round effects already, while leaving optionality to deliver on those hikes later, if required, or for the market to price out hikes should there be another benign shift in energy prices. The demographic profile of the sample is especially important considering that surveys suggest that younger people disapprove of the current government more than older voters (see Figure 15). If a poll overrepresents younger respondents (as is the case with the Datafolha and Quaest surveys in Figure 14), we can assume that the poll will tend to give lower performance for the incumbent, and vice versa if a poll overrepresents older voters. Methodology can also introduce a bias. Telephone or online surveys rely on respondents who are willing to answer the questionnaire and are therefore likely to be more politically engaged. In-person face-to-face street interviews approach people randomly and are thus more likely to reflect the views of the average voter — many of whom, research suggests, become attentive only close to election day. Rising tensions in the Middle East have driven a rebound in oil prices, but absent evidence of a material escalation, we continue to expect the recent move higher to prove temporary as geopolitical concerns gradually subside. Our primary focus remains on Fed policy uncertainty and how different EM countries are positioned to navigate the remainder of the global monetary policy cycle. Figure 2 shows the change in 1 -year implied policy rate expectations since the June FOMC. Markets have priced roughly 30bp of additional tightening in the US, while repricing across most EM countries has been more limited, with Hungary being the notable exception. In our view, this reflects the fact that many EM central banks have generally done a better job containing inflation pressures during this cycle. That said, in an environment of elevated policy uncertainty, we favor countries where rate expectations have repriced more in line with the Fed. We prefer central banks with both the willingness and the credibility to validate or even exceed market expectations. On that basis, our preferred opportunities across the three regions remain COP, KRW, HUF, TRY and ZAR. COP hedges unwind. Our top LATAM conviction trade remains short USDCOP. Favourable external factors: The current environment – in which the market is anticipating potential Fed hikes by year-end, triggering a mild USD strengthening particularly against low-yielding currencies – will remain favorable for the BRL, in our view. Market expectations of a more conservative easing path by Brazil’s central bank, the BCB, due to still unanchored inflation expectations and resilient economic activity, will continue to protect the BRL’s carry advantage. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: The Copom (monetary policy committee) of the BCB delivered a 25bp cut at its June meeting, as we expected, bringing rates to 14.25%. The statement that accompanied the decision had significant changes, mostly aimed at justifying the cut, to signal that the budget of cuts for the year is lower than the Focus survey is currently seeing, and to demonstrate that the bar for hikes is still high, in our view. We anticipate a pause at 14.25% until the December meeting, when the BCB might have the right conditions to return to an easing cycle with a 25bp cut to 14.0% (see Brazil monetary policy: Preparing for a pause, dated 18 June). records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 201/07/2026 The realized volatility in USDINR also impacts the NDS curve. When volatility in USDINR is high, asset holders (such as investors in IGBs and equities) typically increase their hedges by buying USDINR forwards, which pushes the NDS curve higher. During 2023–2024, when USDINR was trading in a tight range, the spread between the NDS and NDOIS curves (FX implied interest rate minus overnight interest rate swap) was trading close to 40bp. However, when the new RBI governor introduced policies that allowed for higher USDINR volatility, it widened to 65bp (Figure 2). RBI measures to push NDS lower: We believe the RBI’s recent measures, particularly those related to Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) rules and external commercial borrowing (ECB), will likely push the NDS curve lower (see FX: RBI, BI try different paths to fight depreciation, dated 12 June). We are currently long INR against EUR (see FX: Sell EURINR, dated 1 July). First, Indian corporates and banks will no longer need to pay NDS to hedge their FX risk when borrowing from the offshore market using ECB. Instead, they will be able to hedge their FX risk with the RBI at a discounted cost, which will not impact the market. We expect USD15– 20bn worth of ECB flows to be routed through this mechanism by the end of the year, significantly reducing paying flow on the NDS curve. Second, we expect

BASE METALS VIEW ▼ The combination of Fed rate hike expectations and uncertain progress towards a peace deal between the US and Iran has created headwinds for most base metals. Aluminium led the way lower in June, down 16% over the month. Copper outperformed the rest of the complex, with prices flat through June as markets awaited an update on US plans for copper tariffs. Looking forward, the resumption of hostilities between the US and Iran, and the consequent rally in oil prices, suggests continued headwinds for the base metals complex. For copper, the US trade department has still not produced a firm tariff decision, suggesting the market will remain in tension. We believe the decision on a refined-copper tariff is likely to be pushed down the road for another six months. For aluminium, we think the market remains fundamentally tight and now looks oversold, with a clear floor around USD3,100/t. Instead, we think policymakers are likely to focus on faster execution of the pro-growth measures – notably those related to fiscal policy – that were mapped out at the National People’s Congress in March. In fact, slow fiscal spending was one of the culprits behind growth deceleration in Q2. Echoing that trend, there was also a slower pace of government bond issuance pace in Q2 compared to the same period last year. records.text: keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 710/07/2026 The potential outcomes in the pension reform debate set out here present an acute risk for France’s indebtedness, more so now than ever. Through this lens, the 2027 presidential election will define the scale of that risk. Should the centre fail to rally around a single candidate heading into the first round, an important tail risk for the market will be LFI ranking second after RN. In this scenario, RN wins the election and the estimates we set out for the party’s proposals in Figure 2 on page 3 become a live prospect, with potentially deep implications for the deficit. Should one of the traditional centrist, left-wing or right- wing parties make it to the second round, that would likely offer more of a challenge to RN given the potential for a re-emergence of a ‘Front Républicain’, the broad alliance historically formed as a bulwark against the far- right. That said, an RN victory in such a scenario is now seen as more likely than in the past (Philippe Marlière, 11 June). If neither RN nor LFI win the election, the most pertinent risk would then lie in the ensuing parliamentary election, and the possibility the result might hamper the new president. IRS 5y5y, meanwhile, has moved above 3.4%, not only a historical high, but also a clear move above the rough textbook calculation for yields – inflation (about 2%) plus real growth (+0.5% in our view). Given this context, our analysis here looks at the potential value in a long position, either outright or versus other rates (curves etc). At this stage, we conclude outright is more monetizable than relative value. We think 10y has become the weakest point in the curve for two reasons. We discussed the first in a 2 July trade idea as the Bank of Japan’s likely extended hiking cycle pushes out the belly of the curve (see Belly shifts from 5y to 10y). The second is that reaction to fiscal risk by the super-long sector has been much mitigated by the finance ministry’s supply cut. 20y also benefited from the supply cut to some extent, but much less than 30y and 40y, so 20y (or 10y10y in IRS) has tended to cheapen more than 5y5y in a fiscal events in 2025. El Niño brings inflationary risks to Emerging Markets El Niño can impact food production and energy generation and drive inflation via food prices and second-round effects. We find Colombia, Peru, and Brazil to be most exposed to in LatAm, and Egypt and South Africa in EEMEA. In EM Asia, we find an impact on food prices, but not headline inflation. In the current juncture, a potentially severe El Niño could compound with elevated fertilizer prices and supply disruptions. Grain supplies could collapse and sugar output shrink Wheat production in Australia has shown near-universal declines during El Niño events and could fall by 20-60% yoy in 2026/27 under an extreme drought scenario. El Niño also puts around 10 mn t (~35%) of Argentina’s wheat output at risk. Meanwhile, Brazil’s corn crop is highly exposed and we expect the 2026/27 harvest to decline by around 10% yoy. Brazil’s sugar output is also at risk and could fall by around 5% yoy in 2026/27. In turn, we see India and Thailand’s combined sugar output declining by at least 10%. records.text: Michael Metcalfe, Caroline Coughlin 13 July 2026 US inflation : Back to normal by the fall? US inflation peaked at just over 5% year -on-year on 31 May before reversing sharply in June. According to State Street PriceStats, the US price level fell 18bps over the month. That may look modest besides the cumulative 3% rise of the previous three months, but outright June declines are rare. Indeed, this is the first monthly fall State Street PriceStats has recorde d since the dataset began in 2008. The impact on annual inflation was larger: it fell 0.5 percentage points over the month, the biggest decline in forty months. More declines are likely. Wholesale oil prices have re -priced somewhat in July after the ceasefire ended but remain well below their peak. As Figures 5 -10 show, this has been only partly reflected in US vehicle fuel prices, suggesting further declines ahead. If June’s fall were repeated through Q3, the State Street PriceStats annual inflation rate would return to 2.7%, its pre-war level, as soon as October, other things equal. Other things, of course, are rarely equal as July is already proving . For now in coming inflation data should be more comfortable, but with the declines driven largely by gasoline prices, much of the move is already anticipated. The consensus expects headline CPI to fall 0.1% month-on-month, seasonally adjusted. Core CPI is also expected to remain well-behaved. The Swiss economy has proved resilient in the face of the energy shock, with timely indicators of economic activity showing that the initial weakness at the onset of the Middle East conflict was short-lived. We think this reflects a diverse energy mix, less energy-intense output, and household electricity prices which are set annually to limit volatility. Meanwhile we continue to see the CHF benefitting from a large current account surplus. This surplus has remained stable despite US tariffs in 2025 and we expect this resilience to continue in 2026 amid higher energy prices. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: The SNB’s decision to keep policy on hold in June at 0% suggests that the monetary policy setting is appropriate for managing the uncertain backdrop. The decision, coupled with recent data releases, ultimately reinforces our conviction that the SNB will remain in a holding pattern for the foreseeable future, as it balances inflationary pressures from the energy price shock and disinflationary pressures from CHF strength, before delivering rate hikes in H2 2027 (see Swiss National Bank: In a holding pattern, dated 18 June). Three-month annualized core inflation has risen to 2.3% from 1.8% a month earlier (Figure 1), while consumer spending remains resilient, as retail sales have increased for five consecutive months through May (Figure 2). Labour market conditions are also tentatively improving. The unemployment rate fell to 6.5% in June, and signs of tightening, alongside limited evidence of broad-based layoffs, point to steady underlying demand. Some of this improvement reflects fewer international students entering the labour force, while youth unemployment has fallen sharply to its lowest level since May 2024. These trends are encouraging for the BoC, although data volatility continues to suggest residual labour market slack. We expect the BoC to leave rates unchanged at its 15 July meeting and to make modest upward revisions to its growth and inflation forecasts in the Monetary Policy Report, while placing greater emphasis on USMCA-related trade risks, which have yet to materialize meaningfully. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 23 July 2026 19 Equity Strategy: Fertilizer availability and economics lead to grain inflation Matthew DeYoe, CFA Research Analyst BofAS Isabella Simonato >> Research Analyst Merrill Lynch (Brazil) The world consumes a number of fertilizers, though at a very high level the industry often aggregates to the 3 primary nutrients; Nitrogen (N), Phosphate (P) and Potash (K). N is produced through hydrocarbon gasification and synthesis, P by mining, leaching (requires sulfur) and chemical synthesis and K by mining and milling. For corn, N is king, and it must be applied annually, while P and K can be thrifted across crops year to year (but not indefinitely) which can create a more volatile demand backdrop. The reliance on hydrocarbons and sulfur for processing (particularly for N and P) has ultimately aligned these businesses with the Middle East, both directly and indirectly. As the Strait of Hormuz closed, 30% of the world’s ocean-going nitrogen and 50% of the world’s ocean- going sulfur has been trapped. This product ultimately sets marginal fertilizer price/costs around the world, and thus has driven material inflation through fertilizer value chains. As fertilizers get more expensive or even face availability shortfalls, farmer consumption declines, creating headwinds to crop production, and ultimately, grain inflation. records.text: Copom minutes raise questions about the durability of the BCB’s hawkish stance. Despite acknowledging a broader inflation deterioration, higher realized inflation, rising expectations, a higher BCB forecast and upside risks from El Niño and pre -election fiscal spending, the BCB still cut rates, suggesting its stance may be softening. Lower oil prices are less supportive for Brazil as a net oil exporter, while the gradual recouping of fuel subsidies limits pass -through to domestic inflation, reinforcing the need for a more hawkish stance than currently signaled. Against this backdrop, we are adding short USDZAR. South Africa should benefit more directly from falling oil prices, improving its external balance and inflation outlook. ZAR had faced the difficult mix of elevated oil prices and softer gold, but commodit y dynamics are now turning more supportive. Oil’s correction toward pre -war levels should lower global inflation expectations and reduce the need for further hawkish repricing, while gold should find support as US real rates stabilize and the recent dollar -driven selloff eases. Together, lower oil and a steadier gold price backdrop create a more favorable setting for ZAR. Brazil and South Africa both remain further from their inflation targets than the Fed (Figure 5), justifying relatively hawkish policy se ttings. TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA 15/07/2026 1 FX: Short USDARS We initiate a short USDARS position as we think that the recent softening in US economic data opens a window for EM FX carry trades to outperform. Among these, the ARS is our top preference as it has the highest carry/vol ratio (Figure 1), with additional trade-channel support expected from the ongoing harvest season and high oil prices. Narrow window for EM carry to perform: The recent decline in the US dollar, sparked by downside surprises in US jobs and inflation figures, has created a favourable environment for EM FX in the short term, particularly for high-yielding currencies like the ARS. Although macroeconomic conditions suggest a risk of ARS depreciation over the medium term, the near-term outlook appears positive for ARS carry trades, in our view. In the next few months, we expect the US dollar to resume its upward trend, driven by anticipated Fed rate hikes, with potentially modest gains against low-yielding currencies (see FX: The USD and rate hikes, dated 9 June). However, we believe that high-yielding currencies like the ARS may be more resilient in this environment, as long as the US dollar does not experience a significant surge, which is not our base case. Harvest and energy prices to support trade balance: We think the final window of Argentina’s harvest season could continue to bolster agricultural exports, generating larger-than-usual USD inflows that should be converted into the ARS in the coming weeks. Hungary expectations set to stay low (for the ‘wrong’ reasons): In CEEMEA, unlike Latam, we expect inflation to surprise to the downside throughout 2027. We forecast the largest surprise in Hungary and the Czech Republic, where we are 0.5pp below consensus for both (on average). Hungary is also the only country in our EM universe where headline inflation (at 1.9% y/y over the last three months) has not only undershot the mid-point of target (3%), but the lower- bound too (2%). Czech does, however, rank high on our reflation risk metrics and we think the central bank is likely to maintain a cautious bias for now. With a relatively high sensitivity to both inflation surprises and past inflation prints, Hungary’s inflation expectations are set to remain lower than those of CEE peers, in our view. The May CPI print marked the fifth consecutive downside surprise, driving the share of consumers expecting prices to fall (i.e. deflation) in the next year to above 12% – an all-time high. Brazil in Latam and Poland in the CEE seem most vulnerable to the contamination of inflation expectations by higher past levels of inflation and inflation surprises. records.text: 1 Insights Market Narratives in Focus: The Case for a Better Summer 14 Jul 2026 Equities. It is summer in the Northern Hemisphere: the sun is out and football is on; one might expect markets to settle into a slow holiday trading rhythm. Unfortunately, not yet. Worries continue to emerge, fortunately our Narrative Map is here to help separate signal from noise. Concerns around market liquidity, commodity prices, and even AI-related capex are attracting far more attention from journalists than from equity investors (top right quadrant in Figure 1). By contrast, narratives around the Fed, inflation, and interest rates remain the key drivers of market direction. Encouragingly, the recent data has been supportive. Our measure of Fed sentiment has turned more dovish alongside the continued decline in inflation (Figure 2). These increasingly benign trends are feeding into a more constructive investor backdrop, reinforcing our positive market outlook and preference for equities and higher-beta portfolios (see our Asset Allocation report for details). So perhaps there is still hope for a happy, relaxed summer after all – at least for equity investors. FX. As with equities, FX markets remain focused on inflation, interest rates, and the Fed’s reaction function (Figure 3). PriceStats indicates that inflation has likely peaked, as discussed in our recent Inflation in Focus piece. The key question now is how the Fed will respond. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW 2 Hawkish Fed drags on prices: Inflation fears have traditionally been seen as a source of support for gold, but markets now focus on the interest-rate implications of higher inflation expectations rather than assessing inflation in isolation. This helps explain why gold prices have struggled in the face of energy-shock-driven price pressures that have prompted a shift in Fed rates calls. Markets now price in one rate hike in 2026 rather than the 2–3 cuts expected before the Middle East conflict. Concerns about rising inflation, among other issues, have been a clear headwind for gold prices through Q2, with front-month CME prices falling from about USD5,400/oz in early March to seven-month lows around USD4,030/oz in mid -June. Since then, though, strong physical market interest, largely in the form of central-bank buying, and investment demand has driven a recovery to a floor around USD4,200/oz. More hikes ahead: Our US economists expect the Fed to reverse the three ‘insurance’ rate cuts made in 2025 at sequential meetings starting this December, with the fed funds rate upper bound expected to reach 4.5% before the end of Q1 next year (see US: Changing our Fed call to rate hikes, dated 5 June). At face value, the University of Michigan sentiment index suggests that US consumers are more pessimistic than they were during the 1970s energy shock, the 2008 financial crisis, and the depths of the Covid pandemic. Yet consumer spending has been robust. We believe the disconnect between what consumers say and what they do comes down to a few main factors: ▪ Index construction: Sentiment gauges do not ask consumers how they feel on a scale of 0 to 100. Instead, they weight specific questions (see Figure 11) intended to assess sentiment via households’ perceived financial health, views on the job market and expectations about future conditions. That is reasonable, but the data shows that what may be dominating, particularly in the Michigan survey, is the perception of inflation or affordability. ▪ Methodological changes: The University of Michigan index appeared to experience a structural break in 2024 with the move to online-only responses. The transition might have shifted the level down nearly nine points (see Cummings and Tedeschi, 2024) ▪ Discontent with high prices: The Michigan measure, in particular, is heavily linked to perceptions about affordability and inflation. However, there is an important caveat – measures of self-employment have risen over recent months (Figure 6). records.text: Dwyfor Evans 22 July 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material South Africa : Fiscal Discipline Meets Monetary Credibility South Africa’s macroeconomic outlook has improved meaningfully over the past year, supported by a stronger policy framework and growing investor confidence. Recent sovereign rating actions by Fitch, S&P and Moody’s reflect progress on fiscal consolidation, debt stabilization, and structural reform. At the same time, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) has strengthened its inflation-targeting regime and reinforced its credibility through a disciplined higher - for-longer policy stance. While rising fuel and commodity prices have reintroduced inflation risks in 2026, elevated real interest rates, improving macroeconomic fundamentals, and continued policy discipline have helped support both the ZAR and the sovereign credit story. This note examines the evolving ratings outlook, the inflation challenge facing the SARB, and why monetary credibility remains central to South Africa’s investment case. The relationship between unemployment and higher interest rates is well-documented. Therefore, it is reasonable to expect some cooling in labour demand following the Bank of England’s fast-paced and pronounced hiking cycle, which it has only partially unwound thus far. The BoE itself estimated in a July 2024 bulletin that a 1pp increase in Bank Rate increases the rate of unemployment by 0.5pp with the peak impact after 1.5 years. Given the bulk of the BoE’s hiking cycle took place from 2022–2023, the timing is consistent with peak labour market cooling (in response to monetary policy) in mid to late 2024, which is evident in the data. However, monetary policy alone cannot explain the dynamics seen over the last few years. Changes to fiscal policy, such as the increase in employer national insurance contributions (NICs), generous national living wage (NLW) increases, and the employment rights bill have indirectly raised firms’ employment costs. According to the BoE’s DMP survey, firms have tried to spread the impact of these policy changes, reducing headcount and allowing profit margins to weaken (Figure 5). records.text: e short-end rates exceed GDP growth, however, liabilities would grow faster than assets and historically you have default cycles and recessions (Figure 2). In the US, that would require rates above 6%, assuming current growth rates. Deteriorating fundamentals: AI-capex is high, hyperscaler cash flow is turning flat, and borrowing has picked up. These are historically warning signs, but for now these cannot be extrapolated to the rest of the market. Figure 3 shows US IG supply by sector versus historical trends. The message here is that the debt capital market is as K-shaped as the economy itself, with clear differences between fast growing industries (tech) and stagnating industries (often more rate sensitive). Why spreads can become extremely tight – Corporate bond scarcity: It may seem far-fetched to discuss corporate-bond scarcity given hyperscalers’ USD170 bn of year-to-date bond sales, but it depends on what you compare with. A credit spread is not just a default-risk premium; it is the spread between two kinds of borrowers: private-sector corporates and governments, and versus abundant government borrowing even hyperscalers pale in comparison. Before the GFC private-sector debt was 75% of US debt; today it is just over half. Corporates have been disciplined, governments profligate. The relative supply between corporates versus governments is, unsurprisingly, closely related to credit spreads over very long periods (Figure 4). Viktor Hjort, Global Head of Credit Strategy
